Hepatology · Cirrhosis

Ascitic Drainage — Paracentesis & Seldinger Drain Insertion

EASL Decompensated Cirrhosis CPG 2018 · AASLD Ascites Practice Guidance 2021 · NUH G&H local practice

Contents

Indications Contraindications Equipment (NUH) Procedure Steps Fluid Investigations Post-Procedure & Albumin
Indications
  • Diagnostic paracentesis: any new-onset ascites; suspected SBP or secondary peritonitis. Mandatory in all hospitalised cirrhotics with ascites.
  • Therapeutic large-volume paracentesis (LVP) / drain: Grade 3 (tense) ascites causing discomfort or dyspnoea, or ascites refractory to diuretics.
Contraindications
Absolute
Overlying skin infection, cellulitis, or abscess at the needle entry site
Bowel distension / obstruction (risk of bowel puncture) — confirm ascites (not gaseous distension) on recent imaging
Lack of patient cooperation without the ability to sedate safely
Relative (discuss with senior)
Coagulopathy (INR >2.5 or platelets <50 ×10⁹/L)
Prior abdominal surgery with extensive adhesions
If there are any concerns about the safety of a bedside procedure (difficult anatomy, loculated/septated ascites, coagulopathy, previous difficult taps), consider referral for IR-guided abdominal drainage instead.
Before inserting a drain for recurrent LVP: check whether previous drains were done at the bedside or by IR — this gives a useful indication of the expected difficulty of the drain and whether IR involvement is likely to be needed again.
Note: Routine correction of INR/platelets is generally not required before paracentesis in cirrhosis — standard coagulation tests overestimate bleeding risk. Confirm thresholds with the proceduralist rather than correcting reflexively.
Equipment — NUH Pericardiocentesis / Drainage Set (Seldinger)

At NUH, ascitic drain insertion uses the pericardiocentesis drainage set via the Seldinger technique. The set contains one dilator only. A separate drainage bag connecting tube is also needed — this joins the drain to an IDC (urine) bag.

Drainage set — Merit Medical Pericardiocentesis Kit (PC801)

8.3 Fr / 40 cm high-flow pigtail catheter. Contains the pigtail catheter, guidewire, access needle, one dilator, scalpel, drape, syringes and a 1000 mL drainage bag.

Connecting tube

The drainage bag connecting tube is packed separately and is what joins the drain to an IDC (urine) bag. Prepare it at the same time as the set.

Connecting tube — front
Connecting tube — reverse (label)

Argon Drainage Bag Connecting Tube, TWS-Male/Funnel (REF 404022000).

Fluid sample bottle
Specimen bottle for ascitic fluid

Label fully before sending. Note that fluid cultures should be inoculated into blood culture bottles — see what to send.

Procedure Steps (Seldinger Technique)
StepAction
1Position patient supine. Confirm ascites on bedside ultrasound. A towel/pillow can elevate the flank so fluid pools in the dependent site. Mark the entry site with the blunt end of a needle.
2Clean and drape with sterile technique. Infiltrate skin and subcutaneous tissue down to the peritoneum with lignocaine 1%; wait 1–2 min. Aspirate while advancing the LA needle — free flow of straw-coloured fluid confirms peritoneal entry depth.
3Insert the introducer needle (syringe loosely attached to allow syringe changes) through the skin with gentle aspiration. Stop when fluid aspirates freely.
4Diagnostic aspirate only: draw ~40 mL into syringes; send samples; remove needle. For a drain: proceed to step 5 after the necessary fluid is drawn.
5Advance the guidewire through the needle into the peritoneal cavity (≥10–15 cm for a stable position). Hold the wire firmly. Remove the needle over the wire, keeping the wire in place.
6Optional scalpel nick: if skin/subcutaneous tissue is thick, make a small skin incision above the guidewire to ease dilator and catheter passage. Apply firm pressure with gauze for minor skin bleeding.
7Thread the single dilator over the wire and advance with a firm twisting motion. Ensure the guidewire is visible from the tail of the dilator before advancing. Remove the dilator while holding the wire. Minor resistance at the fascia is normal — do not force (risk of kinking the wire).
8Thread the drainage catheter over the wire (wire visible from the catheter tail). Advance fully until all fenestrations are within the peritoneal cavity. Remove the wire. Confirm free drainage; aspirate briefly to confirm intracavitary position.
9Secure the catheter with an adhesive dressing. Attach the connecting tubing to a drainage bag. Document the procedure, fluid appearance, and initial volume drained.
Ascitic Fluid Investigations — What to Send

AASLD Practice Guidance — Biggins et al., Hepatology 2021;74(2):1014–1048

A. First Episode / New-Onset Ascites — Comprehensive Workup
TestNotesClinical Value / Threshold
Fluid panel
(mainly fluid protein; includes LDH)		Send with every new tapProtein <15 g/L = high SBP risk → consider prophylaxis if other criteria met. High SAAG + protein >25 g/L → consider cardiac ascites or hepatic outflow obstruction.
Cell count + differential (cytospin)Send with every paracentesis — routine AND newPMN ≥250/mm³ = SBP — treat immediately even without symptoms. Lymphocyte predominance → TB peritonitis, malignancy.
Albumin (ascitic) + paired serum albuminNot included in fluid panel — order separatelySAAG calculation — mandatory for aetiology classification. Both specimens on the same day.
Culture (blood culture bottles)Inoculate ≥10 mL at bedside directly into aerobic + anaerobic bottlesBedside inoculation: sensitivity ~80% vs ~40% for plain tubes. Positive in ~40% of SBP — mostly monomicrobial (E. coli, Klebsiella, S. pneumoniae). Do NOT send in plain containers.
CytologySend ≥50 mL; if malignancy suspectedSensitivity ~60% for peritoneal carcinomatosis. Send if new ascites without known cirrhosis, known malignancy, or unexplained low-SAAG ascites.
AFB smear / culture
+ TB molecular		Add if: low SAAG, lymphocytic ascites, TB-endemic background, immunocompromised, or fever of unknown origin.AFB smear sensitivity ~3% (send anyway). Culture essential — dedicated TB bottle. ADA >36 IU/L supports TB peritonitis.
AmylaseAdd if pancreatic aetiology suspected (pancreatitis, pseudocyst, unexplained pain)Pancreatic ascites: ascitic amylase >3× upper limit of serum amylase.
BilirubinAdd if post-procedure, post-surgery, or bile-stained fluidBiliary ascites: ascitic bilirubin > serum bilirubin — implies biliary leak.
B. Recurrent Ascites / Routine LVP — Simplified Workup

For established cirrhotic ascites undergoing routine LVP (known aetiology):

TestNotes
Cell count + differentialAlways send at every paracentesis — even routine LVP — to rule out SBP.
Culture (blood culture bottles)Send with every paracentesis. Low threshold — bedside inoculation takes minimal time and significantly increases SBP detection.
Add if any concernAlbumin (ascitic + paired serum) if rapid re-accumulation or change in character — re-check SAAG to exclude new non-cirrhotic cause. Cytology if new suspicion of malignancy.
NUH: Inoculate blood culture bottles at bedside — do not send fluid in plain containers. Order ascitic albumin separately from fluid panel (not included by default). Always send cell count + culture at every paracentesis including routine LVP.
Post-Procedure Monitoring & Drain Management
  • Aim to remove all fluid in a single session, but do not keep the drain >72 hours (infection risk).
  • If haemodynamics are a concern, consider limiting drainage to max 2 L/shift. Always clamp the drain if the patient is hypotensive.
  • Hold diuretics while drainage is ongoing.
Albumin replacement (after LVP): when >5 L is drained, ideally 8 g albumin per litre of ascites removed to prevent post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction and AKI. In practice NUH gives 50 mL of 20% albumin per litre drained (which is actually 10 g/L).

Colorectal Polyp Surveillance — Post-Polypectomy Follow-Up

US Multi-Society Task Force on Colorectal Cancer (USMSTF) 2020 · AGA Clinical Practice Update 2020

The surveillance interval depends on the histology, number and size of polyps, the completeness of resection, and the quality of the baseline colonoscopy (adequate prep + complete exam to caecum). If prep is inadequate or the exam incomplete, repeat within 1 year regardless of findings.

If the requested scan uses contrast by default, consider renal function and allergy status (below) before proceeding.

Choosing the Right CT Protocol

Different CT protocols are optimised (by contrast phases and acquisition) for different organs. Choose the right protocol and indicate in the request. Discuss with senior if unsure.

ProtocolTechnique / PhasesIndications / When to Consider
CTAPContrast-enhanced CT abdomen & pelvis. Portal venous phase only is sufficient for most scans (general abdominal survey). An arterial phase is added mainly when active bleeding is suspected, to identify a contrast blush / bleeding point.Default general abdominal scan: undifferentiated pain, collection/abscess, perforation, obstruction, sepsis source, post-op complications, and general oncological staging. For active bleeding → request the arterial phase. In obstructive jaundice → request fine pancreatic cuts (may suffice; a full pancreatic protocol is not always needed — clarify with your senior).
CT PancreasDual-phase: late arterial (pancreatic parenchymal) + portal venous, with thin slices through the pancreas.Suspected/known pancreatic mass; characterising pancreatic lesions; vascular involvement & resectability; pancreatitis complications (necrosis); pancreatic cause of obstructive jaundice.
CT Triphasic LiverArterial + portal venous + delayed phases through the liver (captures hypervascular lesions + washout).Characterising focal liver lesions; HCC diagnosis/surveillance in cirrhosis (LI-RADS); planning liver-directed therapy (resection, ablation, TACE, Y90).
CT Gastric ProtocolCT with gastric distension (water / effervescent) ± multiphasic, optimised for the gastric wall.Gastric cancer staging; gastric wall thickening / known gastric tumour; suspected linitis plastica; tumour extent + nodal disease.
CT — Iodinated Contrast (Contrast-Induced Nephropathy)
ScenarioAction
eGFR 30–59IV NS 1 mL/kg/hr for ≥6H before and after the scan (if no fluid restriction)
Metformin + eGFR 30–60Hold metformin 24H before scan; resume 48H after
AKI (any eGFR)Consider delaying non-urgent CT contrast until AKI resolves
eGFR <30Non-contrast scan or alternative modality. If clinically urgent, counsel on CIN risk using the Mehran risk score (predicts CIN and need for RRT) and document the discussion with the patient ± family.
MRI — Gadolinium (Nephrogenic Systemic Fibrosis)
eGFRAction
>30Safe to proceed
15–30May be permitted after: (1) radiologist–clinician joint decision, (2) patient counselling (NSF risk <0.07%), (3) EPIC SmartPhrase DDINUHMRICKD, (4) order Special Instructions: "CKD 4 with contrast. Counselled for NSF"
<15, or 15–30 with concurrent AKIDiscuss with nephrologist and radiologist. Do not initiate dialysis solely to prevent NSF in eGFR 15–30.
Allergy / Asthma — Premedication
  • Multiple (>3) drug allergies, no contrast allergy: for iodinated contrast, premedicate with PO prednisolone 30 mg the night before + 30 mg the morning of the scan. If urgent, IV hydrocortisone 200 mg ideally 4H before the scan.
  • Contrast allergy: discuss with radiologist re trialling an alternative contrast agent.
  • Asthma: risk of bronchospasm with iodinated contrast — premedicate as for multiple drug allergies and counsel on the risk of an asthma exacerbation.

Key Priorities for Inpatient Care
  • Resuscitate sick patients first. Stabilising the acutely unwell takes priority over administrative and routine tasks.
  • Arrange scopes / procedures promptly. Complete listings and bookings early so time-sensitive procedures are not delayed.
  • Call radiology early for urgent scans. Phone radiology to obtain approval and timing for scans that are needed urgently or early.
  • Keep patients fasted after scans until the result is reviewed, in case a procedure or intervention is needed. Check with the team senior before allowing an oral diet.
  • Keep family updated before invasive procedures. Update family members on the risks and benefits before any invasive procedure — even when the patient has capacity and has consented, provided the patient has agreed for family to be updated.
Portable Ultrasound (Ward 42)

A portable ultrasound machine is available from Ward 42 (e.g. for bedside assessment / marking before paracentesis).

  • Approach the charge nurse in Ward 42 to borrow it.
  • Sign the equipment out in the log book.
  • After use, return it cleaned and sign it back in in the log book.

IR Procedures — Thresholds & Prep

Pre-Procedure Requirements
  • Pre-procedure labs within 1 week: LFTs, FBC, renal panel, coagulation
  • Valid GXM within 72H
  • Request procedure on EPIC; complete IR checklist and fax to IR
  • Speak to IR consultant (Main Building L2, DDI, end of second corridor from the back) to explain indication and request slot
  • Consent patient for procedure
Platelet Transfusion Note
Important: In cirrhotic patients, thrombocytopaenia results from destruction + consumption. Effects of platelet transfusions are short-lived. Avoid transfusing platelets overnight or far in advance — aim to transfuse immediately pre-procedure (e.g. 8am pre AM procedure) or even intra-procedure.

Restarting After the Procedure
Check with the procedurist and read the post-procedure note before restarting any antiplatelet or anticoagulant.
Timing depends on what was actually done and the bleeding risk it created — a diagnostic scope, a large polypectomy, a sphincterotomy and an EMR do not carry the same risk, and the endoscopist may also have left specific instructions (for example after clipping or a bleed treated during the procedure).
If the note does not say, ask the procedurist directly rather than restarting on a default interval.
Reversal: Dabigatran → idarucizumab 5 g IV; dabigatran is also dialysable. Apixaban / rivaroxaban → 4-factor PCC 25–50 U/kg is the practical option; andexanet alfa is not universally available (withdrawn from the US market in December 2025 over thrombotic risk) and does not cover edoxaban. Factor Xa inhibitors are not dialysable.
Always use Cockcroft-Gault CrCl, not eGFR — CKD-EPI/MDRD overestimate renal function in elderly and low-body-weight patients, which makes holds look shorter than they should be.

Gallstone Disease & Choledocholithiasis

ESGE Guideline — Manes et al., Endoscopy 2019;51:472–491
Clinical Presentations
  • Biliary colic: Episodic RUQ/epigastric pain, post-prandial, 30 min–6H, right shoulder radiation. No fever.
  • Acute cholecystitis: RUQ pain + fever + Murphy's sign. Raised WBC/CRP.
  • Choledocholithiasis: Obstructive jaundice — raised ALP/GGT/bilirubin. May be asymptomatic.
  • Cholangitis — Charcot's triad: Fever + jaundice + RUQ pain. Reynolds pentad (severe): + hypotension + confusion.
Natural History — Treat Asymptomatic CBDS?

GallRiks registry (n=3,969): leaving CBDS in situ doubles complications (25.3% vs 12.7%). Even stones <4 mm carry 5.9% complication rate. Offer stone extraction to all patients fit to tolerate it.

Diagnostic Approach — Suspected CBDS
Step 1: Initial tests for all patients
  • LFTs (bilirubin, ALP, ALT/AST, GGT), FBC, CRP, amylase/lipase
  • Abdominal US vs CTAP — US preferred (especially younger patients, avoids radiation), but early CTAP is often easier to schedule at NUH
TestSensitivity for CBDSSpecificityComment
Bilirubin (>22 µmol/L)84%91%Good sensitivity
ALP (>125 U/L)91%79%Most sensitive LFT for CBDS
Abdominal US73%91%Misses small CBD stones
CT (multiphase)78%96%Less accurate for stones <5 mm
Step 2: Intermediate Probability — EUS or MRCP
ModalitySensitivityAdvantagesPrefer When
EUS95–97%Most sensitive; ERCP same session if positiveHigher suspicion of CBD stones — a positive EUS allows ERCP in the same session
MRCP90–93%Non-invasive; whole biliary treeLower suspicion; altered anatomy, pacemaker, claustrophobia, or high sedation risk
Choosing EUS vs MRCP: prefer EUS when suspicion of a CBD stone is higher (a positive EUS allows ERCP in the same session); prefer MRCP when suspicion is lower, sedation risk is high, or anatomy is altered. If a CBD stone is already visible on US/CT → go straight to ERCP (no confirmatory EUS/MRCP needed).
Step 3: Diagnostic algorithm
ScenarioNext Step
Normal LFTs + normal US/CTNo further action
Abnormal LFTs/CBD dilation, no stone visibleEUS or MRCP
CBD stone visible on US/CTProceed directly to ERCP
Acute Cholangitis — Tokyo Guidelines 2018
GradeKey CriteriaDrainage Timing
Grade I (Mild)Does not meet II/III criteria; responds to antibioticsElective (after stabilisation)
Grade II (Moderate)WCC >12 or <4; fever ≥39°C; age ≥75; bili ≥85 µmol/L; albumin <0.7×LLNWithin 48–72H
Grade III (Severe)Organ dysfunction: vasopressors; altered consciousness; PaO₂/FiO₂ <300; Cr >176 µmol/L; INR >1.5; Plt <100ASAP; within 12H if septic shock
Antibiotic Duration in Acute Cholangitis

Adequate biliary drainage is the cornerstone — antibiotics are adjunctive, with early de-escalation once the source is controlled.

  • Source-controlled mild–moderate cholangitis: 3–5 days post-drainage (Am J Gastroenterol 2024).
  • Longer courses only for incomplete drainage, residual stones, or systemic complications.
  • Start broad-spectrum Gram-negative + anaerobic cover (e.g. ceftriaxone + metronidazole).
Post-ERCP Cholecystectomy

All gallstone-disease patients should be considered for cholecystectomy to reduce recurrence. After ERCP for choledocholithiasis, aim for cholecystectomy ideally within 2 weeks (reduces recurrent biliary events and conversion), though this may be difficult to arrange in practice.

ERCP vs PTBD vs Surgery
ModalityPreferred WhenKey Considerations
ERCP (first-line)Standard for most choledocholithiasis/cholangitis. Preferred if anatomy is normal. Internal drainage (no external drain).Requires sedation/GA; higher risk if severely coagulopathic. Check previous surgical history — surgically altered anatomy (e.g. Roux-en-Y, gastric bypass, Billroth II) may preclude conventional ERCP and favour PTBD or a device-assisted/EUS-guided approach.
PTBDERCP not feasible (altered anatomy, failed ERCP); haemodynamically unstable (ICU/HDU) where sedation is high-risk; significant cardiac history making GA prohibitive; intrahepatic ducts dilated.Needs IR expertise + suitable anatomy. May bridge to definitive stone removal once stabilised. Risks: bile leak, haemobilia, tract complications.
Surgical CBD explorationFailed ERCP and PTBD. Lap cholecystectomy + intraoperative cholangiogram if CBD stones suspected at surgery.Rarely first-line. Consider if surgery is needed for another indication (e.g. gangrenous cholecystitis).
ERCP — technical consideration: ERCP is the preferred modality for biliary drainage and stone extraction in choledocholithiasis. Before listing, always review the patient's surgical history — surgically altered anatomy can make conventional ERCP technically not feasible, in which case plan for PTBD, surgery, or a specialised endoscopic approach.
ERCP Antibiotic Prophylaxis (ESGE 2020)
SituationRecommendation
Routine ERCP, low-riskNOT recommended
Anticipated incomplete biliary drainage (PSC, hilar strictures)Recommended

Plastic Biliary Stent

A temporary measure — plastic stents occlude in 3–6 months. Must arrange repeat ERCP for definitive clearance. Document plan before discharge.

IndicationPractical Notes
Irretrievable stonesRepeat ERCP in 4–8 weeks
High bleeding risk precluding sphincterotomyBridge until coagulopathy/anticoagulation managed
Extremely unwell / haemodynamically unstableShort procedure, stent only — full stone clearance deferred
Pancreatic Duct (PD) Stents — Post-ERCP Pancreatitis Prophylaxis

A PD stent may be placed at ERCP to reduce post-ERCP pancreatitis in higher-risk cases (difficult/repeated cannulation, inadvertent PD cannulation/injection, pancreatic sphincterotomy, suspected sphincter of Oddi dysfunction, ampullectomy, young patients) by keeping the PD orifice patent.

  • Biodegradable PD stent: no removal needed — dissolves and passes spontaneously.
  • Non-biodegradable PD stent: may need removal, usually within 1–2 weeks (retained stents risk ductal injury/occlusion).
  • Do an AXR first before arranging removal — many short PD stents pass spontaneously; if not seen on the film, no endoscopic removal is needed.

Acute Pancreatitis

ACG Clinical Guideline — Tenner et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2024;119:419–437 · Boxhoorn et al., Lancet 2020;396:726–734
Diagnosis

Requires ≥2 of 3: (1) typical pain (epigastric/LUQ, radiates to back), (2) lipase or amylase >3× ULN, (3) characteristic CT/MRI findings. Lipase preferred — longer half-life, more sensitive in delayed presentations.

Aetiology & Initial Workup
  • Gallstones (40–70%), alcohol (25–35%). Establish aetiology in all patients.
  • All patients: abdominal US for cholelithiasis
  • Fasting serum triglycerides (TG >11.3 mmol/L = diagnostic), calcium
  • Idiopathic AP: CT pancreas to rule out pancreatic mass (in patients >40 years)
  • Do NOT perform CT routinely on admission — reserve for unclear diagnosis or failure to improve within 48–72H
Severity — BISAP Score

Bedside Index of Severity in Acute Pancreatitis — assessed within the first 24H. Score ≥3 = higher risk of severe AP and increased in-hospital mortality → HDU/ICU. One point each (acronym BISAP). Open BISAP calculator →

LetterParameterThreshold (1 point)
BBUN (urea)Urea >8.9 mmol/L (BUN >25 mg/dL)
IImpaired mental statusGCS <15 (disorientation, drowsiness, stupor or coma)
SSIRS≥2 of 4: temp <36 or >38°C; HR >90; RR >20 (or PaCO₂ <32 mmHg); WCC <4 or >12 ×10⁹/L
AAge>60 years
PPleural effusionPresent on imaging (CXR / CT / US)
Severity cut-off: Score ≥3 within 24H = higher risk of severe AP and increased mortality → consider HDU/ICU. Score <3 = lower risk, ward-based management. Note: Revised Atlanta 2012 also defines severity by persistent organ failure (>48H), which may not be evident at initial scoring — use clinical judgement and reassess regularly.
Fluid Resuscitation
  • Hartmann's solution preferred over normal saline (avoids hyperchloraemic acidosis)
  • Normovolaemic: 1.5 mL/kg/H. Hypovolaemic / hypotensive: fluid boluses titrated and repeated to effect based on haemodynamics, then 1.5 mL/kg/H
  • Goals: HR <120, MAP 65–88 mmHg, UO >0.5–1 mL/kg/H, haematocrit 35–44%
  • Avoid over-resuscitation — risk of abdominal compartment syndrome, pulmonary oedema
Pain Control

A pillar of management alongside fluids and nutrition — inadequate analgesia worsens breathing/atelectasis, mobility and distress. Assess regularly and titrate to effect.

  • Stepwise: regular paracetamol first; add opioids for moderate–severe pain. No good evidence any particular opioid worsens outcomes — do not withhold opioids for fear of sphincter of Oddi effects.
  • Opioids: IV/SC morphine or oxycodone, or PCA for severe pain. Co-prescribe an antiemetic + laxative. NSAIDs with caution (avoid in AKI/volume depletion).
  • Refractory pain: involve the acute pain service; consider PCA or epidural analgesia (may also improve splanchnic perfusion). Reassess for complications (necrosis, pseudocyst, compartment syndrome) if pain escalates unexpectedly.
Nutrition
  • Mild AP: Early oral feeding within 24–48H. Low-fat solid diet — NOT stepwise liquid-to-solid approach.
  • Moderately severe/severe: Enteral nutrition (NG route preferred). TPN only if EN not tolerated.
Role of ERCP
ScenarioERCP?
Biliary AP + acute cholangitisYes — within 24H
Biliary AP + persistent cholestasis, CBD stones confirmedYes — after MRCP/EUS confirmation
Biliary AP + improving LFTs, no cholangitisNo — conservative (APEC trial)
Non-biliary APNo
Local Complications — Revised Atlanta 2012 (Combined)

Banks et al., Gut 2013;62:102–111 · Boxhoorn et al., Lancet 2020;396:726–734

Collections before 4 weeks cannot be fully characterised — manage conservatively. The key clinical distinction: pseudocysts contain only fluid (no solid debris) from interstitial pancreatitis; WON contains solid debris from necrotising pancreatitis.

Cholecystectomy After Biliary AP
  • Mild biliary AP: Same-admission cholecystectomy (PONCHO trial: 5% vs 17% recurrent gallstone events)
  • Severe/necrotising: Delay until collections resolve, or beyond 6 weeks

Singapore context: Local resistance: clarithromycin 17.1%; metronidazole 48.2%; levofloxacin 14.7%.

Bismuth quadruple therapy is now recommended first-line in most international guidelines. However, because of local resistance patterns, clarithromycin triple therapy remains first-line in Singapore (still achieving ~92% eradication locally).

Pre-Treatment Workup

Baseline screening before starting a biologic, thiopurine, methotrexate or long-term steroids.

TestWhy it is done / what to do with the result
IGRA (QuantiFERON)
+ chest X-ray		Latent TB. Anti-TNF increases TB reactivation roughly 5-fold; risk is far lower with vedolizumab and ustekinumab.
Use IGRA, not the tuberculin skin test — Singapore has universal neonatal BCG, and BCG cross-reacts with the Mantoux, giving false positives. IGRA does not.
Positive → treat latent TB first. For anti-TNF and JAK inhibitors, start the biologic only after at least 3–4 weeks of LTBI therapy, and complete the full course. Active TB → delay the biologic by at least 2 months into anti-TB treatment.

Vaccination Checklist

Vaccinate before immunosuppression wherever possible — response rates are better, and the live vaccines become unavailable afterwards.

The timing rule: live vaccines must be given ≥4 weeks before starting immunosuppression, and cannot be given until ≥3 months after stopping it. Non-live vaccines can be given at any time.
VaccineLive?Notes
Hepatitis BNoIf non-immune. Check post-vaccination titre — target anti-HBs >10 IU/mL.
PneumococcalNoA single dose of PCV20 or PCV21 if not previously vaccinated — all adults ≥50, and 19–49 if on immune-modifying therapy. If previously given PCV13/PPSV23, follow the sequencing guidance for an additional dose.
InfluenzaNo (IM)Annually, inactivated.
Zoster — Shingrix
recombinant		NoNot live — safe on immunosuppression. 2 doses. Recommended for all adults ≥50, and from age 19 if on or about to start immune-modifying therapy. In the immunosuppressed the second dose is given at 1–2 months rather than 2–6. Effectively mandatory before a JAK inhibitor.
VaricellaLiveOnly if non-immune, and only ≥4 weeks before starting. Immunity is established by a documented history of chickenpox or a completed 2-dose series — serology is not reliable in someone already vaccinated (high false-negative rate).
HPVNoMale and female. 3-dose schedule in the immunosuppressed regardless of age.
COVID-19NoPer national guidelines. Continue therapy through vaccination.
RSVNoAll patients ≥75; and 50–74 with chronic disease or other risk factors for severe RSV, which includes immunosuppression.
MMR · BCG · yellow fever
oral polio · oral typhoid		LiveContraindicated on immunosuppression — give ≥4 weeks before, or ≥3 months after stopping.
Anti-TNF Drug Levels & Antibodies

A trough level is the drug concentration at its lowest point in the dosing interval — so the sample must be taken immediately before the next dose, before the infliximab infusion is connected or the adalimumab injection is given. Every published target assumes a true trough.

DrugMaintenance target trough
Infliximab≥5 µg/mL (AGA). Aim higher in perianal fistulising disease — commonly quoted as ≥10 µg/mL, though published cut-offs range from about 6 to 20 and none is guideline-endorsed.
Adalimumab≥7.5 µg/mL (AGA).
Interpreting the result in a patient with active disease

First confirm the inflammation is real (CRP, calprotectin, endoscopy). Then the level and antibody result together tell you why the drug is failing, which determines what to do next.

TroughAntibodiesWhat it meansWhat to do
AdequateNoneThe drug is present and still not working — TNF is not driving this diseaseSwitch OUT of class — vedolizumab, ustekinumab, risankizumab, a JAK inhibitor or an S1P modulator
LowNoneUnderdosing, rapid clearance, or non-adherenceDose-escalate or shorten the interval. Ask about missed doses first
LowLow titreImmunogenicity that is often transient and can be overcomeDose-escalate, and add an immunomodulator
LowHigh titre / sustainedImmunogenic failure — the drug is being cleared by antibodiesSwitch. Immunogenicity is drug-specific rather than class-specific, so another anti-TNF with a concomitant immunomodulator is reasonable — but switching out of class is equally acceptable, and is the better option after a second immunogenic failure

Approach to Elevated Bilirubin

Isolated hyperbilirubinaemia (normal ALP, AST, ALT normal or near-normal): distinguish unconjugated causes (haemolysis, Gilbert's syndrome, Crigler-Najjar) from conjugated (hepatocellular disease, intrahepatic or extrahepatic cholestasis).

Cirrhosis — Overview

Ginès et al., Lancet 2021 · Baveno VII 2022 · EASL NITs CPG 2021 · AASLD NILDA 2025
How Cirrhosis Is Diagnosed

Liver biopsy is the historical gold standard for staging fibrosis and diagnosing cirrhosis, but is not always necessary. Its main current role is to determine aetiology in selected cases (e.g. AIH, overlap syndromes, unexplained liver disease) rather than to stage fibrosis routinely when non-invasive tests are available. Standard liver biochemistry and ultrasound alone have sensitivity/specificity <60% for fibrosis staging and are insufficient on their own. In practice, diagnosis combines clinical and imaging features with non-invasive tests.

Natural History
StageKey Features
CompensatedAsymptomatic. Median survival 9–12 years. Annual decompensation risk 4–10%.
DecompensatedAscites, variceal haemorrhage, HE, or non-obstructive jaundice. Median survival ~2 years. Decompensation is driven by portal hypertension, systemic inflammation, and liver failure.
ACLF~30% of hospitalised patients. Acute decompensation + multiple organ failure. ~90% 1-year mortality in advanced ACLF.
Non-Invasive Tests (NITs) for Fibrosis Staging

Two-tier approach: FIB-4 first → FibroScan if intermediate.

TestRule Out Advanced FibrosisIndeterminateRule In Advanced Fibrosis (F3–F4)
FIB-4 (age, AST, ALT, platelets)MASLD: <1.3
Non-MASLD: <1.45		MASLD: 1.3–2.67
Non-MASLD: 1.45–3.25		MASLD: >2.67
Non-MASLD: >3.25
Transient elastography (TE / FibroScan® LSM)<8 kPa (rules out cACLD)8–12 kPa>12–15 kPa (advanced fibrosis); >15 kPa highly suggestive of cACLD
MR elastography (MRE)Better sensitivity/specificity than TE—Most accurate imaging NIT; not routine — expensive and limited availability

Performance reduced by: obesity (use XL probe), food intake within 2H (perform fasted), hepatic congestion, biliary obstruction, significant hepatic inflammation (all falsely elevate LSM). Not applicable in decompensated cirrhosis.

Disease Severity Scores
ScoreComponentsKey Thresholds
CTPAlbumin, bilirubin, INR, ascites, HEA (5–6): low risk · B (7–9) · C (10–15): high risk/surgical risk
MELDBilirubin (µmol/L), INR, creatinine (µmol/L)≥15: consider LT listing · 40: <3-month survival without LT
MELD-NaMELD + serum sodiumUsed for LT allocation; lower Na → higher priority
General Management Principles
  • Treat the cause: Alcohol abstinence, HBV suppression, HCV cure, weight loss in MASLD
  • Nutrition: 35 kcal/kg/day; protein 1.2–1.5 g/kg/day; bedtime snack to minimise overnight fast
  • Drugs to avoid: NSAIDs (AKI risk in ascites), ACE-I/ARB (hypotension and AKI in ascites). Paracetamol safe ≤2 g/day. Statins safe in compensated cirrhosis at low doses (e.g. simvastatin 20 mg ON).
  • Vaccinations: HAV, HBV, pneumococcal (PCV13 + PPSV23), annual influenza
  • HCC surveillance: Ultrasound ± AFP every 6 months
  • Transplant referral: MELD ≥15 or any decompensation — refer early if the patient is eligible (no absolute contraindication, e.g. active malignancy, uncontrolled sepsis, ongoing substance use, or prohibitive comorbidity)
Documenting the Cirrhosis Issues List

Keep a structured cirrhosis issues list in the daily ward round note and the discharge summary, updated daily to reflect the latest management/investigations. For every cirrhotic patient, document:

  • Severity + aetiology: CTP and MELD scores with the aetiology — e.g. "CTP B7, MELD 15, MASH cirrhosis"; update the scoring daily as the patient's condition changes
  • Basis of diagnosis: biopsy (if done), FibroScan/LSM, imaging, supportive clinical/endoscopic features
  • Ascites: known ascites + grade; prior LVPs (SAAG, fluid protein, dates); diuretic dose, or the reason not on diuretics
  • Variceal bleeding: known varices + any bleeds; most recent OGD (date + findings); NSBB dose, or the reason not on an NSBB
  • HCC: known HCC; date of last cross-sectional imaging + AFP; if present, the latest treatment + HPB MTB recommendations
  • HE: prior HE; on lactulose and/or rifaximin

Diagnostic Paracentesis — Ascitic Fluid Investigations

Diagnostic paracentesis is the single most important investigation in new ascites. Consider it in new-onset Grade 2–3 ascites, and in hospitalised cirrhotic patients with ascites — particularly on admission, or if there is any clinical deterioration. The decision is a clinical one and depends on the wider picture. The SAAG classifies aetiology with ~97% accuracy.

SAAG = Serum albumin − Ascitic albumin (both same-day specimens)

SAAGMechanismCauses
≥11 g/L (High SAAG)Portal hypertensionCirrhosis (most common), cardiac failure/constrictive pericarditis, Budd-Chiari, portal vein thrombosis, massive liver metastases
<11 g/L (Low SAAG)Not portal hypertensionPeritoneal carcinomatosis, TB peritonitis, nephrotic syndrome, pancreatitis, bowel obstruction/infarction, biliary ascites

AASLD Practice Guidance — Biggins et al., Hepatology 2021;74(2):1014–1048

Diagnostic paracentesis is mandatory for all new-onset Grade 2–3 ascites and in all hospitalised cirrhotic patients with ascites. The SAAG (serum albumin − ascitic albumin) classifies ascites aetiology with ~97% accuracy.

What to send: the full list of ascitic fluid investigations (new-onset comprehensive workup vs routine-LVP simplified workup, SBP thresholds, and NUH sampling notes) is in the Ascitic Drainage chapter.
Definitions & Grading

Ascites is the most common cause of decompensation (~5–10% of compensated patients per year). 5-year survival falls from ~80% (compensated) to ~30% (ascites present).

SAAG Interpretation & Ascites Classification
GradeClinical FeaturesManagement
Grade 1 (Mild)Ultrasound onlySodium restriction. No evidence treatment modifies natural history.
Grade 2 (Moderate)Symmetrical distension, shifting dullnessNa restriction (80–120 mmol/day) + stepwise diuretics
Grade 3 (Tense)Marked distension, fluid waveLVP + albumin. Diuretics to prevent re-accumulation.
Key Terminology
TermDefinition
Uncomplicated ascitesNot infected, not refractory, not associated with HRS
Refractory ascitesCannot be mobilised or recurs rapidly despite maximal medical therapy
Diuretic-resistantNo response to Na restriction + max diuretics (spironolactone 400 mg + furosemide 160 mg/day)
Diuretic-intractableDiuretic complications (HE, Na <125, AKI, K disturbance) preclude effective diuretic doses
Diuretic Approach

Na restriction: 80–120 mmol/day (no-added-salt diet). Target weight loss: ≤0.5 kg/day (no oedema) or ≤1 kg/day (with oedema).

Patient CategoryStrategy
First episode, preserved renal functionStart spironolactone alone (practically 25 mg OM; guidelines suggest 100 mg/day upfront) → titrate every ≥72H → max 400 mg/day. If no response or hyperkalaemia: add furosemide 40 mg/day → max 160 mg/day.
Recurrent / long-standingCombination from outset: spironolactone 50 mg + furosemide 20 mg together → titrate every ≥72H → max spironolactone 400 mg + furosemide 160 mg/day.
Diuretic Hold Criteria
ComplicationAction
Na <125 mmol/LWithhold ALL diuretics
AKI or progressive renal impairmentWithhold ALL diuretics
Overt HE (no other precipitant)Consider holding
K <3 mmol/LStop furosemide; correct hypokalaemia
K >6 mmol/LStop spironolactone
Grade 3 — Large Volume Paracentesis (LVP)
  • Remove all fluid in single session. Avoid drain >72H (infection risk).
  • Albumin replacement if >5 L removed: ideally 8 g per litre drained; in practice NUH gives 50 mL of 20% albumin per litre drained (which is actually 10 g/L)
Refractory Ascites
  • Repeated LVP: first-line therapy
  • TIPSS: indicated if eligible (see TIPSS section for contraindications)
  • Consider liver transplantation
SBP — Diagnosis

Diagnostic paracentesis in all hospitalised cirrhotic patients with ascites + any of: GI bleeding, fever, AKI, or hepatic encephalopathy. Send: cell count, cultures (≥10 mL into blood culture bottles), total protein and albumin.

CategoryCriteriaAction
SBP (culture-positive)PMN ≥250/mm³ AND positive cultureTreat immediately
Culture-negative SBPPMN ≥250/mm³ AND negative culture (~60%)Treat identically to SBP
BacterascitesPMN <250/mm³ AND positive cultureIf symptomatic: treat. If asymptomatic: repeat tap.
Secondary peritonitisMultiple organisms, very high PMN/protein, localised symptomsCT abdomen; surgical review

Empirical antibiotics: IV ceftriaxone — culture-directed thereafter. Total duration 5–7 days.

Albumin (mandatory): 20% albumin 1.5 g/kg IV Day 1 → 1 g/kg Day 3. Reduces HRS-AKI 30% → 10%, mortality 29% → 10% (Sort et al., NEJM 1999).

SBP Prophylaxis
IndicationRegimen
Acute GI haemorrhageCeftriaxone 1 g/24H IV × 7 days
Primary: ascitic protein <15 g/L + Child-Pugh ≥9 with bili ≥51 µmol/L OR impaired renal function OR Na ≤130Ciprofloxacin 500 mg OM
Secondary: previous SBPCiprofloxacin 500 mg OM (reduces recurrence 68% → 20%)

Updated HRS Nomenclature

HRS = kidney dysfunction in cirrhosis + ascites, with reduced GFR in the absence of structural kidney disease (no proteinuria >500 mg/day, no microhaematuria, normal renal US). Requires exclusion of other causes including hypovolaemia (no improvement after diuretic withdrawal + albumin challenge).

Old TermNew Term (ICA 2023)Definition
Type 1 HRSHRS-AKIAKI criteria met. No response to diuretic withdrawal + 2-day albumin challenge.
Type 2 HRSHRS-AKDeGFR <60 for <3 months. No AKI criteria.
—HRS-CKDeGFR <60 for ≥3 months.
AKI Staging (Adapted KDIGO / ICA)
StageCreatinine Criteria (µmol/L)
Stage 1ARise ≥26.5 within 48H OR ≥1.5–2× baseline; peak SCr <133
Stage 1BAs Stage 1; peak SCr ≥133
Stage 2>2–3× baseline SCr
Stage 3>3× baseline OR SCr ≥353.6 with acute rise ≥26.5 OR RRT initiated
AKI/HRS Management Flowchart
Approach to AKI and HRS in Cirrhosis (NEJM 2018 / Gut 2015)
General AKI Management (All Stages)
  • Consider an indwelling urinary catheter for strict input/output monitoring.
  • Withhold diuretics and beta-blockers.
  • Stop nephrotoxic drugs (NSAIDs, vasodilators, aminoglycosides, contrast where possible).
  • Screen and treat all infections actively.
  • Exclude intrinsic renal causes: send UFEME and urine protein:creatinine ratio (UPCR) — active sediment / significant proteinuria suggests intrinsic (e.g. ATN, glomerular) rather than HRS.
  • Exclude post-renal / obstructive causes: post-void residual (bladder scan) for bladder outlet obstruction; ultrasound kidneys, ureters & bladder (US KUB) for hydronephrosis / obstruction.
  • If tense ascites + AKI: therapeutic paracentesis to rule out SBP; consider LVP to reduce abdominal compartment pressure.
  • If no obvious cause OR AKI ≥Stage 1B: 20% albumin 1 g/kg/day (max 100 g) × 2 days (albumin challenge).
  • Monitor fluid status carefully while giving albumin — watch for volume overload / pulmonary oedema, especially with concurrent oliguria or cardiac dysfunction.
HRS-AKI Treatment
TreatmentDetails
Terlipressin + albumin FIRST-LINETerlipressin — continuous 24H IV infusion is the NUH approach (rather than intermittent bolus dosing). Start 2 mg/24H by continuous infusion; if SCr fails to fall ≥25% after 48H, uptitrate stepwise to a maximum of 12 mg/24H. Continuous infusion achieves comparable efficacy to bolus dosing with fewer adverse events.
Albumin: 20–40 g/day IV.
Duration: until complete response, or maximum 14 days.
Pre-treatment: ECG. Watch for ischaemic events.
RRTFor non-responders with standard RRT indications. Base on disease severity and LT candidacy.
Liver transplantationDefinitive treatment. Allocate using pre-treatment MELD. SLK: RRT ≥4 weeks OR eGFR ≤35 mL/min sustained ≥4 weeks.

Response: Complete = SCr within 26.5 µmol/L of baseline. Partial = regression ≥1 stage but SCr still elevated. Recurrence after cessation: re-treat with same regimen.

Monitor volume status carefully while on terlipressin. Terlipressin combined with daily albumin readily precipitates pulmonary oedema — a leading cause of treatment discontinuation and of respiratory failure in HRS-AKI. Review fluid balance, oxygen saturation and respiratory examination at least daily; consider reducing or withholding the albumin dose at the first sign of volume overload, and stop terlipressin if pulmonary oedema develops. Also watch for ischaemic complications (digital, mesenteric, cardiac) and hyponatraemia.

Screening for Varices

Screening identifies patients with high-risk varices who require primary prophylaxis. In compensated cirrhosis, a patient already established on a non-selective beta-blocker does not require screening endoscopy, as the result would not alter management. A patient on a selective beta-blocker may be switched to a non-selective agent where appropriate.

Compensated cirrhosis — start with LSM and platelets
LSM + plateletsWhat it meansAction
LSM <20 kPa AND platelets >150High-risk varices ruled outNo endoscopy needed. Repeat LSM + platelets yearly.
LSM ≥25 kPaCSPH highly likelyStart NSBB (no prior endoscopy required).
Anything in between
the grey zone — e.g. LSM 20–25 with platelets <150, or LSM 15–20 with platelets <110		CSPH cannot be confidently ruled in or outOffer screening endoscopy.
How often to repeat the scope
SituationInterval
On an NSBBNo surveillance endoscopy required
Decompensated cirrhosisAnnually
Compensated, no varices seenEvery 2 years if liver injury is ongoing (still drinking, untreated hepatitis)
Every 3 years if quiescent (abstinent, HCV cured)
High-risk varices found, started on an NSBB, no bleedingNo follow-up endoscopy required
Any new decompensating event — new or worsening ascites, encephalopathy, jaundice or bleeding — is an indication to repeat the OGD, rather than waiting for the next scheduled interval.
Primary Prophylaxis
FindingTreatmentSurveillance OGD (if not on NSBB)
No varices, no CSPHNo NSBB — surveillance onlyEvery 2 years if liver injury is ongoing; every 3 years if quiescent
CSPH, no varicesCarvedilol — the indication is CSPH itself, not the presence of varices—
Small varicesCarvedilol. Band ligation is not technically feasible for small varices.Every 1 year if liver disease uncontrolled; every 2 years if controlled
Medium or large varicesCarvedilol or band ligation. NSBB is preferred (it also prevents ascites and other decompensation), but banding is a reasonable alternative and remains procedurist-dependent. Band ligation is the option if an NSBB is contraindicated or not tolerated.Every 1 year if uncontrolled; every 2 years if controlled
NSBB Dosing & Cautions
DrugDosing
CarvedilolStart 3.125 mg BD → increase to 6.25 mg BD after 2–3 days if tolerated. Do not titrate to heart rate — carvedilol lowers portal pressure at low doses. Start lower in Child-Pugh B/C. Step back down to 3.125 mg BD if systolic BP <90 mmHg.
Ascites is not a contraindication, but dose-reduce or stop if systolic BP is persistently <90 mmHg or HRS-AKI develops.

Absolute contraindications: 2nd/3rd degree heart block without pacemaker; poorly controlled asthma; severe peripheral arterial disease; uncontrolled heart failure; bradycardia (HR <50 bpm).

Stop during AKI or proven SBP.

Acute Variceal Haemorrhage (AVH)

6-week mortality 15–25%. Start vasoactive drugs as soon as AVH suspected — before endoscopy.

StepActions
ResuscitationTwo large-bore IV. Target Hb 7–9 g/dL (restrictive — do NOT over-transfuse). Avoid colloids. Intubate if Grade 3–4 HE before OGD.
Vasoactive Drugs (IMMEDIATELY)Somatostatin 250 mcg IV bolus → 250 mcg/hr infusion. Continue 2–5 days.
AntibioticsCeftriaxone 1 g/24H IV × 7 days. Reduces bacterial infections, rebleeding, and mortality.
OGDWithin 12H (unstable). Within 24H (most). EBL for oesophageal varices. Cyanoacrylate for gastric varices. Erythromycin 250 mg IV 30 min before scope.
Pre-emptive TIPSS (within 72H)Consider if: Child-Pugh C (score <14) OR Child-Pugh B + active bleeding at index OGD. Reduces treatment failure and mortality (Garcia-Pagan, NEJM 2010). See TIPSS chapter →
Failure/RebleedRepeat OGD. If fails: salvage TIPSS. Bridge with balloon tamponade (Sengstaken-Blakemore).
Secondary Prophylaxis (After First Bleed)
  • Carvedilol/NSBB + EVL in combination — standard of care.
  • Repeat banding every 2–4 weeks until the varices are obliterated.
  • After obliteration: OGD at 6 months, then every 12 months indefinitely, to detect recurrent varices.
  • Continue the NSBB indefinitely. Banding treats the varices; the NSBB treats the portal pressure. Stop only for persistently low BP or severe intolerance — and if you do stop, re-scope to look for high-risk varices needing banding.
  • NSBB is not required after TIPSS if the portosystemic gradient is <12 mmHg.
  • Consider LT evaluation after a first variceal bleed in decompensated cirrhosis.

HVPG — Measuring Portal Pressure

The hepatic venous pressure gradient is the reference standard for measuring portal pressure. A catheter is passed via the jugular vein into a hepatic vein and a balloon is inflated to occlude it: HVPG = occluded ("wedged") pressure − free hepatic vein pressure. A gradient is used rather than absolute pressures because it cancels out the patient's volume status and intra-abdominal pressure.

HVPGMeaning
1–5 mmHgNormal
>5 mmHgPortal hypertension
≥10 mmHgCSPH Clinically significant portal hypertension — the threshold that matters. Predicts varices, decompensation and HCC. Below 10 mmHg, ~90% will not decompensate over 4 years.
≥12 mmHgVariceal bleeding threshold — bleeding essentially does not occur below this
In practice HVPG is not routinely measured. CSPH is usually inferred non-invasively from liver stiffness and platelet count using the Baveno VII criteria above, and NSBBs are started on clinical grounds regardless of whether HVPG is available.
Where HVPG is misleading

HVPG only measures the pressure drop across the sinusoid. It is accurate in cirrhosis — but can be normal despite severe portal hypertension when the obstruction lies elsewhere.

Site of obstructionExamplesHVPG
Pre-hepaticPortal or splenic vein thrombosisNormal — the block is upstream of the liver
Intra-hepatic —
pre-sinusoidal		Schistosomiasis · congenital hepatic fibrosis · early PBC · sarcoidosis · PSVD / non-cirrhotic portal hypertension · nodular regenerative hyperplasiaNormal or mildly ↑ — underestimates the true portal pressure
Intra-hepatic —
sinusoidal		Cirrhosis · alcohol-associated hepatitis↑↑ — accurate
Intra-hepatic —
post-sinusoidal		Sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (veno-occlusive disease)↑ — the obstruction lies within the segment being measured
Post-hepaticBudd-Chiari · IVC obstruction · constrictive pericarditis · right heart failureNormal — both pressures rise together and cancel out. A raised free hepatic vein pressure is the clue

Hepatic Encephalopathy (HE)

West Haven Grading
GradeCategoryClinical Features
0–1CovertGrade 1: trivial lack of awareness, euphoria/anxiety, impaired calculation, shortened attention span.
2Overt HELethargy, disorientation (time), personality change, constructional apraxia.
3Overt HESomnolence, responsive to stimuli. Gross disorientation, asterixis.
4Overt HEComa; unresponsive. Decerebrate posturing may be present.
Precipitants to Identify & Treat
  • GI bleeding (most common) — examine stool, OGD if indicated
  • Infection/sepsis — blood cultures, urine culture, diagnostic paracentesis
  • Constipation, dietary protein excess
  • AKI or electrolyte disturbance (hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia)
  • Drugs: benzodiazepines, opioids, sedatives, diuretics
  • Porto-systemic shunts or TIPSS dysfunction
Screening for Covert HE

Covert HE (West Haven grade 0–1) is not clinically obvious and needs psychometric or computerised testing. Useful in patients with cirrhosis who have subtle cognitive complaints, impaired driving/work performance, or before activities requiring vigilance.

TestHow to AdministerNormal vs Abnormal
Stroop test
(EncephalApp — free on the App Store / Google Play)		App-based. Patient names the colour of discordant colour-words across “Off” and “On” runs. Records completion times.Abnormal if OffTime + OnTime > ~190–275 s (varies with norms/age). Longer total time = worse performance → suggests covert HE.
Number Connection Test Part A (NCT-A)Paper test — patient joins numbers 1→25 in sequence as fast as possible; record time in seconds. Download and print a copy for the patient (see figure below).Roughly: <30 s normal; 30–50 s borderline; >50–60 s abnormal (age-dependent — use local/age norms). Slower completion suggests covert HE.
Number Connection Test — Part A (print for patient)

Source: Zeegen R, Drinkwater JE, Dawson AM. Method for measuring cerebral dysfunction in patients with liver disease. Br Med J. 1970;2(5710):633–6.

Treatment
  • Lactulose: First-line. Titrate to 2–3 soft stools/day. Use IV/PR if unable to take orally.
  • Rifaximin 550 mg BD: Add for recurrent HE (≥2 overt episodes). Reduces HE recurrence ~58% (LoE I).
  • Nutrition: Do NOT restrict protein. Target 1.2–1.5 g/kg/day. Small frequent meals + late-night snack.
  • Airway: Grade 3–4 HE — assess need for intubation especially pre-OGD.
  • Avoid: Benzodiazepines, opioids, sedatives.
Ordering a lactulose enema (EPIC): order lactulose and change the route of administration to “use as specified”. Under comments, write: “mix 20 mL of lactulose with 100 mL of water and administer as enema.” Remember to order an enema bottle as well.
NUH note: Rifaximin 550 mg BD available on NUH formulary. Document prior HE episodes clearly.

BCLC 2026 Staging Diagram

Treatment Modalities — What Each One Involves
ModalityWhat it actually is
ResectionSurgical removal of the tumour-bearing segment(s). Curative. The limiting factor is not the tumour but how much functioning liver is left behind.
Thermal ablation
RFA / MWA		A needle electrode is placed into the tumour percutaneously under imaging guidance and the tumour is burnt — using radiofrequency (RFA) or microwave (MWA) energy. Curative for small tumours, and far less invasive than surgery.
TACE
Transarterial chemoembolisation		IR catheterises the hepatic artery branch feeding the tumour and injects chemotherapy together with embolic particles. HCC is supplied almost entirely by the hepatic artery whereas normal liver is supplied mainly by the portal vein — so the tumour is starved and dosed while the rest of the liver is largely spared. Not curative; a disease-control treatment, usually repeated.
Y90 / TARE
Radioembolisation, "SIRT"		Same arterial route as TACE, but the particles injected are radioactive yttrium-90 microspheres — internal radiotherapy delivered directly into the tumour's blood supply. Requires a planning angiogram and lung-shunt scan first. Used when TACE is unsuitable, or to ablate a single tumour ("radiation segmentectomy").
SBRT / EBRTExternal beam radiotherapy tightly focused on the tumour. A non-invasive alternative when ablation is not technically feasible.
Liver transplantTreats the tumour and the underlying cirrhosis — the best long-term outcome, but limited by tumour burden criteria and organ availability.
Systemic therapyImmune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) — antibodies that take the brakes off the immune system (atezolizumab, durvalumab, nivolumab); given in combination, now first-line. Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) — oral anti-angiogenic drugs (sorafenib, lenvatinib); now mainly second-line or when ICIs are contraindicated.

Y90 Radioembolisation (SIRT) — Pre-Treatment Workup

NUH IR Protocol · EASL CPG HCC 2025 · ACR-SIR Practice Parameter 2022

Y90 requires a two-stage process: a planning procedure followed by the actual treatment. The planning procedure is essential to assess anatomy, tumour vascularity, and lung shunting before proceeding.

StepInvestigation / ActionPurpose
1. Cross-sectional imagingCTTAP (contrast CT thorax-abdomen-pelvis) + CT liver volumetric (volume segmentation)Stage tumour; rule out extrahepatic disease; assess tumour size, location, vascular anatomy; calculate target and non-target liver volumes for dosimetry.
2. Planning angiogramIR hepatic angiogram (diagnostic arteriography)Map arterial anatomy; identify tumour-feeding vessels; identify and coil aberrant vessels supplying bowel/stomach (prevents radiation gastritis/ulceration); confirm technical feasibility.
3. Lung shunt fraction (LSF)NM Tc-99m MAA lung shunting scan (SPECT/CT)Simulates Y90 microsphere distribution to estimate how much would shunt to the lungs. A higher LSF means more dose reaches the lungs — used to adjust or, if very high, contraindicate Y90 (radiation pneumonitis risk).
4. LabsLFT, FBC, coagulation (INR <1.5, Plt >50), bilirubin <51 μmol/L preferred, renal functionAssess liver reserve and procedural safety thresholds.

Portal Vein Thrombosis (PVT)

AASLD Practice Guidance — Northup et al., Hepatology 2021;73(1):366–413. Nomenclature per AASLD 2020 standardised terminology: "recent" preferred over "acute".

Contents

Nomenclature & Classification Aetiology & Workup Management — Non-Cirrhotic Management — Cirrhotic
Nomenclature & Classification

The term "recent" is preferred to "acute" per AASLD 2020 standardised nomenclature. "Acute" implies both symptoms and recent onset — not all patients with new PVT develop symptoms, and precise dating is often impossible without prior imaging.

TermAASLD 2020 DefinitionKey Features
Recent PVTPVT presumed present for <6 monthsNo established portoportal collaterals. May be symptomatic (abdominal pain, fever, mesenteric ischaemia) or incidental. Previously called "acute PVT" — this term should no longer be used.
Chronic PVT / Cavernous transformationPVT present or persistent for >6 months. When portoportal collaterals are established, the preferred term is "cavernous transformation of the portal vein".Recanalization that does not occur within 6 months is unlikely to occur thereafter. Non-cirrhotic chronic PVT = EHPVO (extrahepatic portal vein obstruction).
Completely occlusiveNo persistent lumenOcclusion extent important for management decisions and LT planning
Partially occlusiveClot obstructing >50% of original lumen
Minimally occlusiveClot obstructing <50% of original lumen
Tumour PVTHCC vascular invasion — arterial enhancement on CT/MRI. Not bland thrombus.Classify as BCLC C; systemic therapy. Must be excluded before managing as bland PVT.
Aetiology & Workup
  • Cirrhosis — most common in Asia. Severity of portal hypertension and low portal vein velocity (<10–15 cm/s) are key risk factors.
  • Myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs): JAK2 V617F mutation in ~30–40% of non-cirrhotic PVT — screen ALL non-cirrhotic PVT without a clear provoking factor
  • Inherited thrombophilias (Factor V Leiden, Prothrombin G20210A, Protein C/S deficiency, antithrombin deficiency), APS, PNH, intraabdominal inflammation (pancreatitis, IBD, appendicitis), OCP, pregnancy, surgery
  • >35% of non-cirrhotic PVT: no identifiable risk factor found
WorkupWhenNotes
Doppler US → CT triphasic or contrast MRIAll PVTExclude tumour thrombus (HCC invasion) — mandatory before any management decision. Arterial enhancement in thrombus = tumour PVT.
Thrombophilia screenAll non-cirrhotic PVT without clear provoking factorJAK2 V617F · Protein C and Protein S · antithrombin · Factor V Leiden · antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin IgG and IgM, anti-β2-glycoprotein I IgG and IgM).
Thrombophilia screen in cirrhosisNot routinely recommendedResults rarely change management in cirrhosis. Consider only if strong family history or unusual clinical features.
Management — Non-Cirrhotic PVT
ScenarioApproachDuration
Recent PVT + intestinal ischaemiaSurgical emergency. Immediate anticoagulation (LMWH). Urgent surgical/IR/critical care consultation. Thrombolysis only if ischaemia persists despite anticoagulation.Ongoing — reassess
Recent PVT, no ischaemiaAnticoagulate to prevent thrombus extension and promote recanalization. LMWH → DOAC or warfarin when stable. EVL can be performed safely without stopping anticoagulation. Aim to start early — recanalization better with <6 months.Minimum 3–6 months. If recanalization achieved + provoking cause resolved: consider stopping.
Unprovoked / MPN-associatedIndefinite anticoagulation. MPN: cytoreduction (haematology) + anticoagulation.Indefinite
Chronic PVT / cavernous transformation (non-cirrhotic)No established benefit of anticoagulation in established cavernous transformation without active thrombosis. Manage portal hypertension complications.No routine anticoagulation
PVT in Cirrhosis
ScenarioManagement
Recent PVT, complete or partially occlusive (>50%), LT candidateAnticoagulate (LMWH; DOACs in CP-A/B). Treat high-risk varices first (EVL). Indefinite until LT. Repeat imaging every 2–3 months on therapy to assess treatment response.
Recent PVT, minimally occlusive (<50%), LT candidateSerial imaging every 3 months. If progressive → anticoagulate. Observation reasonable if stable.
Recent PVT, not an LT candidateAnticoagulate if benefits outweigh risks (risk of progression, portal hypertension worsening). Discuss case-by-case.
Chronic PVT / cavernous transformation, cirrhoticNo established benefit of anticoagulation for established cavernous transformation. Target management of portal hypertension complications. Alert transplant team — TIPSS-PVR may be considered in LT candidates.
Anticoagulant choiceLMWH or DOACs (CP-A/B with adequate renal function). Avoid DOACs in CP-C, severe renal impairment, or active variceal bleeding. Warfarin: use chromogenic Factor X assay (not INR) for monitoring in cirrhosis.
TIPSS-PVR (portal vein recanalization)Consider in LT candidates with chronic PVT/cavernous transformation that would prevent physiological anastomosis. Also for recurrent bleeding/refractory ascites with PVT not amenable to anticoagulation.

TIPSS

AASLD Portal Hypertension Guidance 2024 · EASL Decompensated Cirrhosis 2018 · Baveno VII 2022

Contents

What Is a TIPSS? Pressure Targets Indications Contraindications Pre-Procedural Workup Complications
What Is a TIPSS?

A transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt is a stent placed by interventional radiology between a hepatic vein and an intrahepatic branch of the portal vein, creating a low-resistance channel that diverts portal venous flow into the systemic circulation.

The portosystemic pressure gradient falls, reducing the risk of variceal bleeding and the rate of ascites re-accumulation. Because portal blood bypasses the hepatic sinusoids, first-pass hepatic metabolism is reduced and cardiac preload is increased — hence hepatic encephalopathy in 30–50%, hepatic decompensation and cardiac decompensation. Decompression is therefore titrated to a target gradient rather than maximised.

Pressure Targets

IR measures the portosystemic pressure gradient (PSG) — portal vein pressure minus IVC pressure — before and after the stent is placed. It typically falls from around 20 mmHg to about 8 mmHg.

IndicationTarget PSG
Variceal bleeding<12 mmHg, or a ≥50% reduction from baseline. Below 12 mmHg, portal hypertensive bleeding is very unlikely.
Refractory ascitesNo agreed target — guidelines decline to specify one. Recent data favour roughly 8–11 mmHg: going lower adds encephalopathy and liver failure without further benefit.
Indications
IndicationDetails
AVH — Pre-emptive (within 72H)Child-Pugh C (<14) OR Child-Pugh B + active bleeding at index OGD
AVH — SalvageFailed 2 sessions of endoscopic haemostasis
Secondary prophylaxisIntolerant to/fails NSBBs + EVL. PTFE-covered stent preferred.
Refractory ascitesFailed maximal diuretics. Prefer in younger CP-A/early CP-B, no HE, awaiting LT.
Hepatic hydrothoraxRefractory transudate
Budd-Chiari SyndromeAfter failed anticoagulation + angioplasty. Bridge to LT in fulminant cases.
Contraindications
CategoryDetails
AbsoluteRight heart failure or severe PAH (mean PAP >45 mmHg). Uncontrolled HE (grade ≥2). Uncontrolled systemic infection. Untreated biliary obstruction. Complete PVT with no recanalisable segment.
RelativeSevere liver failure (bili >51 µmol/L + INR >2 + CP-C >12). HE grade 1–2 (individualised). MELD >18 without LT candidacy. Age >70 with comorbidities.
Pre-Procedural Workup
InvestigationPurpose
FBC, coagulation, LFTs, renal panelMELD calculation. Correct INR >2.5 or Plt <30 before procedure.
CT abdomen triphasic or MRI liverExclude HCC, delineate vascular anatomy (portal vein patency, flow, hepatic vein anatomy) — mandatory
EchocardiogramExclude right heart failure / pulmonary hypertension (TIPSS significantly increases preload)
Cognitive / HE assessmentBaseline West Haven grade. Grade ≥2 = major risk factor for post-TIPSS HE.
Complications
ComplicationIncidenceManagement
Hepatic Encephalopathy20–45%Lactulose + rifaximin. If refractory: shunt reduction by IR.
TIPSS Dysfunction/Stenosis~20% at 1 year (PTFE-covered)Doppler ultrasound at 1, 3 and 6 months, then 6-monthly. Angioplasty/restenting if stenosis.
Liver Failure5–20%Supportive. Expedite LT. Can reduce/occlude shunt.
Right Heart Failure<5% if echo normalDiuresis; escalate to cardiology. Shunt reduction if refractory.

Hepatitis B Reactivation Prophylaxis

AGA Clinical Practice Guideline on the Prevention and Treatment of Hepatitis B Virus Reactivation in At-Risk Individuals — Ali FS et al., Gastroenterology 2025;168:267–284.
AGA Clinical Decision Support Tool: HBV Reactivation (Figure 2)

Contents

What Reactivation Is Step 1 — Baseline Testing Step 2 — Risk Stratification Corticosteroids Step 3 — Prophylaxis or Monitoring Choice of Antiviral, Timing and Duration Monitoring Without Prophylaxis Caveats When Applying the Algorithm
What Reactivation Is

Hepatitis B virus reactivation (HBVr) is the loss of immunological control of hepatitis B under immunosuppression. It occurs in patients who are HBsAg positive (chronic infection) and in those who are HBsAg negative with a positive anti-HBc (resolved infection, in whom viral DNA persists within the hepatocyte nucleus).

HBV-DNA rises first; a hepatitis flare may follow weeks later, sometimes only after the immunosuppressive agent has been withdrawn. Flares range from an asymptomatic transaminitis to acute liver failure, and commonly interrupt the treatment the patient requires. Reactivation is largely preventable, so risk is assessed before therapy begins — from the patient’s serological status and the immunosuppressive exposure, which the algorithm above combines.

Step 1 — Baseline Testing

The AGA makes a strong recommendation to test for hepatitis B in anyone about to receive a therapy that carries reactivation risk. Because the CDC now advises universal screening of all adults aged 18 and over, stratifying who gets screened by the magnitude of risk is no longer necessary — test everyone before immunosuppression.

  • Minimum serology: HBsAg and total anti-HBc. Add anti-HBs, since it identifies patients who need vaccinating.
  • HBV-DNA if HBsAg and/or anti-HBc is positive.
ResultInterpretationAction
HBsAg positiveChronic HBV infectionHighest reactivation risk. Assess the exposure against the table below. Also assess whether the patient meets criteria for HBV treatment in their own right.
HBsAg negative, anti-HBc positiveResolved infectionStill at risk. Risk is lower than in HBsAg-positive patients for most exposures, but is high with B cell–depleting agents.
HBsAg negative, anti-HBc negativeNo previous exposureNot at risk of reactivation. Vaccinate if anti-HBs is also negative.

A patient who independently meets criteria for hepatitis B treatment under standard guidelines should receive antiviral therapy regardless of their reactivation risk category.

Step 2 — Risk Stratification

Risk is the expected incidence of reactivation without prophylaxis: high >10%, moderate 1–10%, low <1%. Read the row for the drug the patient is about to receive, then the column for their serology.

ExposureHBsAg positiveHBsAg negative /

Corticosteroids

Steroid risk depends on dose and duration, not on the steroid alone. Doses are prednisolone or equivalent per day: low <10 mg, moderate 10–20 mg, high >20 mg.

Dose and durationHBsAg positiveHBsAg negative /
anti-HBc positive
Moderate or high dose, ≥4 weeksHighModerate
Low dose, ≥4 weeksModerateLow

Intra-articular injectionLowLow

A short reducing course of prednisolone therefore does not require prophylaxis, whereas the four-week high-dose course commonly given with chemotherapy or for a severe autoimmune flare does.

Step 3 — Prophylaxis or Monitoring
RiskRecommendationStrength
High >10%Antiviral prophylaxis rather than monitoring aloneStrong, moderate certainty
Moderate 1–10%Antiviral prophylaxis rather than monitoring aloneConditional, moderate certainty
Low <1%Monitoring alone rather than antiviral prophylaxisConditional, moderate certainty

The conditional recommendations allow for individual preference. A moderate-risk patient who places a high value on avoiding long-term medication and its cost may reasonably choose monitoring instead, provided adherence to that monitoring is realistic. Conversely, a low-risk patient who is exposed to more than one low-risk agent, or in whom reliable follow-up cannot be guaranteed, may reasonably be given prophylaxis.

Choice of Antiviral, Timing and Duration
  • Use an agent with a high barrier to resistance — entecavir, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate or tenofovir alafenamide. The efficacy data underpinning the recommendations assume such an agent; lamivudine has a low barrier to resistance and is not appropriate for this purpose.
  • Start before the risk-imposing therapy begins, not alongside it.
  • Continue for at least 6 months after the risk-imposing therapy is stopped.
  • At least 12 months after stopping a B cell–depleting agent, because reactivation has been reported well beyond the six-month point.
  • In HCV co-infection treated with direct-acting antivirals, it is reasonable to continue prophylaxis for 6–12 months after the DAA course rather than stopping with it — reactivation has occurred shortly after the antiviral was withdrawn.
Monitoring Without Prophylaxis

Where monitoring alone is chosen, it must be structured, and it must be arranged before treatment begins.

  • Every 1 to 3 months, for the duration of the risk-imposing state.
  • HBV-DNA and ALT together. ALT alone is inadequate — the viral load rises first, and treating at that point prevents the flare rather than reacting to it.
  • Start an antiviral immediately if HBV-DNA becomes detectable or rises.
Caveats When Applying the Algorithm
  • Do not use anti-HBs to decide. A positive surface antibody does not reliably protect against reactivation, and the AGA explicitly states that it should not be used to guide prophylaxis in any risk group. Anti-HBs is useful for deciding whether to vaccinate, not for deciding whether to prophylax.
  • Risk from multiple agents is cumulative. Most patients receive combinations — the table gives the risk of single exposures, and a regimen combining several moderate-risk drugs, or any drug with a four-week course of steroids, sits higher than the individual rows suggest.
  • The estimates apply to the duration of the risk-imposing state, or up to one year. Risk over longer exposures is less certain.
  • Reassess if the regimen changes. A patient categorised as low risk who is later escalated to rituximab moves to the highest category and needs prophylaxis started.

Parenteral Nutrition

Singapore clinical guideline on parenteral nutrition in adult patients — Lum JHM et al., Ann Acad Med Singap 2025;54:350–368 · NICE CG32 · ASPEN Consensus Recommendations for Refeeding Syndrome 2020

Contents

When PN Is (and Is Not) Appropriate Referral Workflow Before Starting — Access & Baseline Labs Monitoring on PN Refeeding Syndrome

Parenteral nutrition (PN) is the intravenous administration of an admixture containing dextrose, amino acids, lipid emulsion, electrolytes, vitamins and trace elements, bypassing the gastrointestinal tract entirely.

Enteral nutrition (EN) is preferred wherever the gastrointestinal tract is functional and accessible. EN is more physiological, preserves mucosal integrity and gut barrier function, is considerably less costly, and carries fewer complications. PN is associated with catheter-related bloodstream infection and thrombosis, metabolic and electrolyte derangement, hyperglycaemia and hepatobiliary dysfunction. PN should therefore be reserved for patients in whom oral and enteral intake cannot meet nutritional requirements, and should not be commenced until pragmatic measures to improve oral or enteral tolerance have been exhausted.

When PN Is (and Is Not) Appropriate

PN is indicated in patients who are unable to meet their nutritional requirements orally and/or enterally as a result of suboptimal gastrointestinal function, or in whom the gastrointestinal tract is not accessible. The Singapore guideline groups these into five broad categories:

CategoryExamples
Impaired absorption or loss of nutrientsShort bowel syndrome · extensive small bowel resection · high-output enterocutaneous fistula or stoma · severe malabsorption (radiation enteritis, extensive Crohn's disease)
Mechanical bowel obstructionMalignant bowel obstruction · adhesional obstruction not amenable to early operative management · stricturing Crohn's disease
Clinical need for bowel restProximal high-output fistula · gastrointestinal anastomotic leak · mesenteric ischaemia · severe acute pancreatitis where enteral feeding is not tolerated
Bowel motility disordersProlonged post-operative ileus · chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction · severe gastroparesis refractory to post-pyloric feeding
Inability to achieve or maintain enteral accessFailed or unsafe placement of a nasoenteric or post-pyloric tube · altered anatomy precluding enteral access · repeated tube dislodgement in a patient unable to meet requirements orally
Nutritional statusWhen to start
Well nourishedConsider PN after 5–7 days of not achieving ≥60% of estimated energy requirement.
Severely malnourished or at high risk of malnutritionConsider PN earlier than 5 days of not achieving ≥60% of estimated energy requirement.

Open the MUST calculator to screen for malnutrition risk.

Contraindications — do not start PN if:
• Critical electrolyte abnormalities — K <2.5 mmol/L, Na <125 mmol/L, PO₄ <0.4 mmol/L or Mg <0.5 mmol/L. Correct these first, then start.
• No suitable venous access.
• Irreversible brain injury or terminal illness where there is no therapeutic goal of prolonging life.
Referral Workflow
  1. Put up a dietitian referral on EPIC — state parenteral nutrition as the reason for referral.
  2. Call the gastroenterology senior resident covering the nutrition service (check the roster).
Refer early in the day. PN bags have to be ordered and compounded, so refer ideally before 11am — the hard cut-off is 12pm on weekdays. A referral after the cut-off means the patient will not receive PN that day.
Before Starting — Access & Baseline Labs
Venous access
  • A PICC with a dedicated lumen is the recommended access for PN. An existing central venous access device in the internal jugular vein may be used for up to 14 days.
  • Peripheral PN is only a supplemental option where oral/enteral intake is suboptimal, and should not exceed 14 days. Osmolarity must be kept <900 mOsm/L for peripheral use.
  • Flush the line with normal saline after each use, or weekly if not in use.
Baseline bloods before initiation
PanelIncludes
RenalSodium, potassium, creatinine, urea, bicarbonate, chloride
Bone / mineralsCalcium, phosphate, magnesium — also the electrolytes that define refeeding risk
LiverALP, ALT, AST, GGT, bilirubin
LipidsLipid profile, including triglycerides
GlucoseBaseline capillary or serum glucose
Monitoring on PN
WhatHow oftenTarget / action
Blood glucoseEvery 6 hours for at least the first 48 hoursTarget 7.8–10 mmol/L. Use subcutaneous insulin rather than adding insulin to the bag. May stop 6-hourly monitoring in non-diabetics who stay normoglycaemic without insulin at target rate.
Electrolytes
Na, K, PO₄, Mg, Ca		Daily for the first few days if at risk of refeeding; reduce once stableCorrect abnormalities promptly.
Liver functionBaseline, then weekly; reduce if normalDeranged LFTs are usually multifactorial — look for non-PN causes first (sepsis, drugs, biliary obstruction). Overfeeding also causes them.
TriglyceridesWith routine bloodsKeep <4.6 mmol/L. If above, reduce dextrose then lipid. Stop PN if >11.4 mmol/L.
Line complications. If catheter-related bloodstream infection is suspected, take two sets of blood cultures — one from the line and one peripheral — before starting antibiotics. Complicated infection means the line comes out.
Refeeding Syndrome

Definition (ASPEN 2020): a measurable fall in phosphate, potassium and/or magnesium, or the appearance of thiamine deficiency, developing within hours to days of restarting or substantially increasing calories in someone who has been undernourished. It occurs within 5 days of feeding.

SeverityFall in PO₄, K and/or Mg
Mild10–20%
Moderate20–30%
Severe>30%, and/or organ dysfunction from the electrolyte fall or from thiamine deficiency
Who is at risk

High risk if any one of: BMI <16 · unintentional weight loss >15% in 3–6 months · little or no intake for >10 days · low K, PO₄ or Mg before feeding. Or any two of: BMI <18.5 · weight loss >10% in 3–6 months · little or no intake for >5 days · history of alcohol misuse, or drugs including insulin, chemotherapy, antacids or diuretics. (NICE CG32)

High-risk conditions to think of: anorexia nervosa and other eating disorders, chronic alcohol use, prolonged fasting, malabsorption (short bowel, Crohn's, pancreatic insufficiency), post-bariatric surgery, cancer, prolonged vomiting or hyperemesis, major surgery without nutrition support.
If at risk
  • Start low. Begin PN at 15–20 kcal/kg/day and advance progressively.
  • Consider IV thiamine 100 mg OM for 3–5 days.
  • Check K, PO₄ and Mg before starting and monitor daily for the first few days. Replace promptly.
  • Multivitamins and trace elements are added to the PN bag.

Bleeder On Call — Workflow

Who Is the Bleeder On Call?

Every day, either a Gastro registrar or a GS registrar + a gastro/GS consultant are rostered as the bleeder on call. Details found on Rooster.

Indications for Referral

Large BGIT (upper or lower GI bleed) with or without haemodynamic instability.

Information to Have Before Calling
  • Indication: site (upper vs lower), nature (haematemesis, melaena, haematochezia, PR bleed)
  • Last meal — timing of last oral intake (ideally fasted for ≥6H before scope for airway safety)
  • Comorbidities / baseline: key cardiac, renal and respiratory issues — these affect resuscitation, sedation/airway risk and transfusion thresholds
  • Haemodynamics and airway status — the most critical piece of information. Determines immediate actions and whether resuscitation must precede the referral call.
  • Lab results: Hb, urea, creatinine and their trends (allows GBS calculation)
  • Antiplatelets/anticoagulants in use and suitability for reversal — may require haematology referral
Resuscitation — Immediate Steps by Scenario
ScenarioAction
Peri-arrest / extreme haemodynamic instabilityConsider Code Blue activation ± MTP (Massive Transfusion Protocol). Resuscitate with blood products (PCT). Do not delay resuscitation to make the referral — do both simultaneously.
Large bleed with haemodynamic compromise2× large-bore IV access. Fluid resuscitation / blood products. Consider ICU referral. Transfusion threshold: Hb <7 g/dL (8 g/dL if cardiac disease).
Airway at risk (massive UGIB, altered consciousness, Grade 3–4 HE)Early ICU referral — consider intubation for airway protection, especially pre-OGD.
Haemodynamically stable, small bleedMay be suitable for early scope next morning rather than overnight — discuss with bleeder on call. Daytime has better logistical support.
Suitability for Scopes
  • Haemodynamically unstable patients: resuscitation takes priority over endoscopic evaluation
  • Initial resuscitation and airway protection must be instituted before patient is suitable for scopes
  • Once stable: OGD within 12H for suspected varices or ongoing instability; within 24H for most UGIB
Medications to Prepare Pre-scope
  • IV PPI: Esomeprazole 80 mg bolus → 8 mg/hr (if peptic ulcer suspected)
  • Somatostatin: 250 mcg bolus → 250 mcg/hr if variceal bleeding suspected — start before OGD
  • Antibiotics (cirrhosis + GI bleed): Ceftriaxone 1 g/24H IV × 7 days
  • Erythromycin 250 mg IV ~30 min before scope — prokinetic to clear gastric blood/clot and improve visualisation. Timing and use should be guided by the senior / bleeder registrar.
Other Preparation Needed
  • Keep Nil By Mouth (NBM) — in preparation for endoscopy and to protect the airway.
  • Two large-bore IV cannulas (≥18G) for resuscitation and transfusion.
  • Send/repeat FBC, coagulation, renal panel, GXM; ensure valid group & crossmatch.
Anticoagulant / Antiplatelet Review
  • Hold all anticoagulants. DOAC reversal is usually decided in consultation with haematology — specific agents: idarucizumab (dabigatran), andexanet alfa (apixaban/rivaroxaban taken within 24H).
  • Warfarin: hold and give vitamin K. If life-threatening bleed → 4-factor PCC (e.g. Beriplex/Prothrombinex) for rapid reversal (FFP only if PCC unavailable).
  • High cardiac risk (recent stent / ACS on DAPT): hold DAPT for the acute bleed, but restart as soon as possible once haemostasis is secured and/or after discussion with cardiology — stent thrombosis risk rises with prolonged interruption. Aspirin can usually be restarted immediately after endoscopy.
  • Complex or competing-risk decisions: early haematology ± cardiology referral.
After the Bleed — Handover

Bleeders managed overnight are handed back to the respective gastro teams for review during morning rounds, and should be followed up daily until the team senior has decided for PRN review. Document: endoscopic findings, interventions, post-procedure medication plan (PPI, vasoactives, antibiotics), and any repeat scope plan.

If you are the inpatient gastroenterology team reviewing a post-bleeder patient: you are responsible for ensuring any planned scope for the day is consented and listed, and that the endoscopy centre is called to confirm the listing.
