Gastroenterology

Upper GI Bleeding (UGIB)

ACG Clinical Guideline — Laine et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2021;116:899–917
Definitions

UGIB originates proximal to the ligament of Treitz (oesophagus, stomach, duodenum).

  • Haematemesis: vomiting fresh or coffee-ground blood
  • Melaena: black, tarry stool (requires ≥50–100 mL blood in the upper GI tract)
  • Haematochezia: bright red PR bleeding — may indicate massive UGIB
Aetiology
  • Peptic ulcer disease — most common (30–40%)
  • Oesophageal or gastric varices
  • Mallory-Weiss tear
  • Oesophagitis / erosive gastritis
  • Upper GI malignancy
  • Dieulafoy lesion, angioectasia, aorto-enteric fistula (less common; consider aorto-enteric fistula after prior aortic surgery)
Risk stratification: the Glasgow-Blatchford Score (GBS) stratifies pre-endoscopic risk — GBS 0–1 very low risk (may avoid admission); GBS ≥2 → admit and scope within 24H. Open GBS calculator →
Initial Management
  • IV access: Two large-bore cannulas; fluid resuscitate if haemodynamically unstable
  • Transfusion: RBC at Hb <7 g/dL (8 g/dL if cardiac disease)
  • Erythromycin 250 mg IV: 20–30 min before OGD
  • Pre-endoscopic PPI: IV esomeprazole 80 mg bolus → 8 mg/hr
  • Somatostatin: 250 mcg bolus → 250 mcg/hr if suspected variceal bleeding
  • Ceftriaxone 1 g IV: in patients with a history of cirrhosis presenting with UGIB (suspected variceal bleed) — antibiotic prophylaxis reduces infection and mortality
  • Timing of OGD: Within 24H; <12H if haemodynamically unstable or suspected varices
Forrest Classification
ClassAppearanceRebleed RiskTreat?
IaActive spurting>80%YES
IbActive oozing~50%YES
IIaNon-bleeding visible vessel40–50%YES
IIbAdherent clot~25%Attempt clot removal
IIcFlat spot~8%No endoscopic Rx
IIIClean base~3%No endoscopic Rx
Post-Endoscopic PPI (Peptic Ulcer)
  • High-risk (Ia/Ib/IIa/IIb): IV PPI (esomeprazole 80 mg bolus → 8 mg/hr × 72H) then oral PPI BD. The 72H is counted from the time of endoscopic haemostasis / intervention, not from admission.
  • Low-risk (IIc/III): Oral PPI BD; consider early discharge
  • Identify the underlying cause of PUD: check H. pylori status (was a CLO test or histology taken? — if not done at the index scope, plan it at repeat endoscopy or arrange an outpatient UBT) and review NSAID use.
  • Repeat endoscopy: most gastric ulcers require a repeat OGD in ~8 weeks to confirm mucosal healing (and exclude malignancy).
  • Recurrent bleeding after endoscopic therapy: consider repeat endoscopic treatment; if not amenable or haemostasis fails → IR angioembolisation or surgery.
NUH note: H. pylori testing at time of scope (CLO test). If positive, eradication on discharge. Repeat OGD 6–8 weeks for gastric ulcers.

Consent

Contents

Completing the Consent Form Risks & Alternatives
Completing the Consent Form
Spell everything out in full — no abbreviations anywhere on the consent form. Write “Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy”, not “OGD”; “Endoscopic Variceal Ligation”, not “EVL”; “keep in view therapeutics”, not “KIV therapeutics”. This applies to the procedure name, the procedure-specific description and any free text.

Complete the consent form on EPIC. For an OGD:

  • Procedure: Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy keep in view therapeutics — written out in full.
  • Always consent for “keep in view therapeutics” for every procedure, so therapeutic intervention can proceed in the same sitting if needed.
  • Procedure Specific Description: NUHS Endoscopy Information for OGD (search SmartText — description must start with “NUHS Endoscopy”).
  • Sedation — always select “Yes”. Explicitly counsel sedation risks (cardiorespiratory depression, aspiration, and the small risk of AMI/stroke) in addition to the procedure itself.
  • Anaesthesia — select “Yes” if the procedure is under GA/MAC.
Named therapeutics — “therapeutics” alone is not always enough. Where a specific intervention is anticipated it must be named in the consent.
• Always consent for Endoscopic Variceal Ligation in cirrhotic patients going for an OGD — write the procedure in full, e.g. Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy keep in view therapeutics keep in view Endoscopic Variceal Ligation.
• Endoscopic Variceal Ligation risks must be specifically counselled and added as free text into the Procedure Specific Description (free-text add-on to the OGD procedure-specific description): pain, perforation 0.1%, oesophageal stricture 0–2%, infection 0–3.3%, bleeding ≤3.5%.
Consent — SmartText lookup for the OGD risk form
Consent details — procedure + procedure-specific description

Complete the consenting-person section (mark Q18 / authorising person appropriately) and the doctor’s declaration.

Consent — consenting/authorising person + declaration
Consent — cross-institutional listing + declaration
Consent — signature (patient + explaining doctor)
Consultant consent (patient without mental capacity): single consultant consent — amend Q18 and the Authorising Person; the consultant signs as Explaining Doctor (single signature only).

ProcedureRisks (key)Alternatives
OGDPerforation 0.03–0.05%; Bleeding 0–0.1%; Overall ≤0.1%Barium swallow; observation
EVLPain; Perforation 0.1%; Oesophageal stricture 0–2%; Infection 0–3.3%; Bleeding ≤3.5%Medications alone (inferior for variceal bleed)
ColonoscopyMortality 0.007%; Post-polypectomy syndrome ≤0.1% (if electrocoagulation used); Perforation ≤0.3%; Bleeding ≤2% (higher on antiplatelets)CT colonography; barium enema; observation
EUS ± FNAPerforation 0.06%; with FNA: Bleeding 0–0.5%, Infection 0–1.4%, Pancreatitis 0.2–2%; Overall ≤2.5%US/CT/MRI; CT- or US-guided biopsy; observation
ERCPInfection 0.1%; Perforation 0.6%; Bleeding 1.3%; Pancreatitis 3.5%PTBD (external drainage)
Liver BiopsyPain 84%; Infection 14%; Vasovagal 3%; Pneumothorax <1%; Bleeding 0.5%; Organ damage 0.1%; Haemobilia 0.05%; Death 0.11%; Needle-tract seeding 0.003–0.009%Holding off on biopsy — but this risks missing the diagnosis and losing the ability to provide targeted treatment

All consents must cover: description of the procedure, intended aim, risks, alternatives, and an opportunity for the patient to ask questions and clarify misconceptions.

Bowel Preparation (Colonoscopy)
Diet modification

Low-residue diet ordered on EPIC, at least 1 day before the scope (start earlier if endoscopy is anticipated).

  • Morning scopes (0830–1300): low-residue diet ≥1 day before · clear feeds at dinner the day before · NBM from 2359 the day before (apart from bowel prep solution).
  • Afternoon scopes (1330–1700): low-residue diet ≥1 day before · clear feeds breakfast to finish by 0700 on the day · NBM from 0700 on the day (apart from bowel prep solution).
Bowel prep regimens
PrepMorning scopeAfternoon scopeCautions
PEG3 L from 1400 after lunch the day before; 1 L from 0600 on the day2 L from 1400 after lunch the day before; 2 L from 0600 on the dayCHF; severe renal impairment (eGFR <30)
Picoprep1 sachet at 1900 the day before + 5 × 250 mL water over 2–3H; 1 sachet from 0600 on the day + 3 × 250 mL water over 1–2H1 sachet at 1900 the day before + 5 × 250 mL water; 1 sachet from 0900 on the day + 3 × 250 mL waterCHF; eGFR <30; GI ulceration; rhabdomyolysis; hypermagnesaemia

Last dose should start within 5H of the appointment and finish ≥2H before the appointment time.

Troubleshooting: inadequate prep on the morning of the scope (and ≥2H available) → give an extra 1 L PEG immediately; consider a fleet enema (lactulose enema if renal impairment). Not tolerating prep → small sips of clear drinks to aid taste if no contraindication.
Pre-procedure Precautions
  • Check for loose teeth before endoscopy — loose teeth will require dental extraction prior to the procedure.
  • Pacemakers, ICDs and loop recorders need pre-procedure assessment — see Cardiac Devices (CIED) below.
  • Hold iron supplements 5–7 days before colonoscopy; hold SGLT2 inhibitors 3 days before scopes.
  • Check antiplatelet / anticoagulant use — see the Antithrombotic chapter for hold durations.
Cardiac Devices (CIED) Before Endoscopy

Applies to any patient with a pacemaker, ICD or loop recorder having gastroscopy, colonoscopy, EUS, ERCP or bronchoscopy.

1. Identify the device and refer
  • Establish four things: device and manufacturer · defibrillator status · pacing dependence · procedure site (DDPP).
  • Contact the cardiac registrar — their recommendations are entered into EPIC.
    Inpatient: registrar covering the patient's location. Outpatient: registrar covering KRW/DSOT.
  • Biotronik pacemakers: review the magnet response specifically — it is not the same across manufacturers.
A loop recorder only records — no action is required.
2. Is the patient pacing dependent?

Read it off the ECG: pacemaker spikes in front of all or most P waves and/or QRS complexes means the patient is pacing dependent. What happens next depends on this and on whether the device also defibrillates.

No defibrillator function
pacemaker only		Has defibrillator function
ICD
Pacing dependentReprogram to asynchronous pacing (VOO/DOO 80).Reprogram the ICD:
• asynchronous pacing (VOO/DOO 80)
• disable tachycardia therapies
• maintain tachycardia sensing
Continuous ECG monitoring for ventricular arrhythmias. External defibrillation if unstable ventricular arrhythmia is detected. Reprogram to usual settings after endoscopy.
Not pacing dependentHave a magnet immediately available in case pacing becomes inhibited or the patient becomes pacing dependent.Place a magnet over the device to disable anti-tachycardia therapy.
Continuous ECG monitoring for ventricular arrhythmias.
If an unstable ventricular arrhythmia occurs — remove the magnet so the device can detect and defibrillate.
External defibrillation if no therapy is delivered.
Remove the magnet after endoscopy.
3. During the procedure
  • Transcutaneous defibrillation pads in the anterior/posterior position, >8 cm from the device, as backup defibrillation for ICDs.
  • Monitor closely with plethysmography for pacing inhibition.
  • Use bipolar cautery wherever possible. If unipolar electrocautery is used, keep to short bursts <5 seconds.
  • Place the electrocautery return patch as far from the device as possible.
  • Prophylactic antibiotics are NOT indicated for a CIED.
4. After the procedure
A device check is required if either applies:
• the device was reprogrammed before the procedure — it must also be returned to its usual settings; or
• there was intraprocedural cardiac arrest, CPR, temporary pacing, or external electrical cardioversion.

Adapted from the NUHCS protocol for CIED patients undergoing endoscopic procedures (Nov 2023).

Endocentre List (Snapboard)
  • Go to Snapboard (in the ribbon at the top of the EPIC window).
  • Select “NUH Endo” to view the endoscopy list (each column = one scope room; patients listed chronologically).
  • Hovering over a patient’s name opens a popup with additional details, including the endoscopist.
Room 2 is the inpatient endoscopy room — the inpatient list is run there in the morning. Inpatient cases are listed in Room 2, so check there for available slots. This includes: inpatient gastro/hepato/transplant patients; patients under other disciplines seen as blue letters; and bleeders (if listed early enough and there is space in the list).
Snapboard — select “NUH Endo”
Ordering Procedures (using OGD as an example)

Order “OGD” (or the relevant procedure) on EPIC. Where the order goes depends on whether the scope is for an inpatient or an outpatient:

  • Inpatient procedures → order under Inpatient Orders on EPIC.
  • Outpatient procedures → order under Discharge Orders on EPIC.

Search for the procedure by name or by its order code — the code is shown against the order in EPIC (visible in the screenshots below):

  • OGD: SF701I — Intestine/Stomach, Upper GI Endoscopy With/Without Biopsy [1B]
  • Colonoscopy: SF702C — Colon, Colonoscopy, Fibreoptic With/Without Biopsy [2C]

Complete the order as below.

For inpatient scopes:
• Emergency/elective → set to “Emergency” (not “Elective”) so the scope is picked up on the inpatient list.
• Consultant Performing Specialty → “NUH Gastroenterology”.
OGD order — Emergency + Consultant Performing Specialty = NUH Gastroenterology

The order summary panel (right) should reflect: Emergency, Consultant Performing Specialty = NUH Gastroenterology, and the chosen anaesthesia requirement.

Colonoscopy order — same Emergency + NUH Gastroenterology fields
  • Consultant (inpatient scope): inpatient endoscopy consultant for the day — find on Rooster (gastroenterology monthly roster, scroll right). Also visible on the Provider Calendar — see below.
Provider Calendar — Inpatient Endoscopy registrar / consultant
  • Consultant (outpatient scope): primary team consultant, or the consultant whose list the scope is listed under — confirm with team SR/consultant.
  • Confirm the listing by phone: Inpatient 67722317 · Outpatient 67726388.
  • Colonoscopy: also order bowel prep (inpatient or discharge depending on timing).
  • ERCP: also order “RF Fluoro” at the same time. Standard order — SF710B: Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) with Sphincterotomy / Removal of Stone / Insertion of Biliary Stent [3C].
  • EUS: SF718B — Endoscopic Ultrasound without Fine Needle Aspiration [2C] (e.g. when looking for choledocholithiasis); SF717B — Endoscopic Ultrasound with Fine Needle Aspiration [3A] (for FNA/B).
Confirm the scope is actually listed: after calling, double-check on Snapboard that the procedure has been listed. Listing order/timing is not always sequential — avoid scheduling scans or off-ward activities on the morning of a scope, as the endocentre may fetch the patient early.
Arranging for GA / MAC
  • Most procedures are done under sedation, but selected patients may require GA/MAC.
  • When ordering the procedure, choose the appropriate option (GA vs MAC).
Booking the date — order of calls
  1. Call the anaesthesia clerk @ 67724208 and ask for the dates on which anaesthesia is able to support the procedure.
  2. Take those dates to the procedurist and check which of them fits his or her schedule.
  3. Call the anaesthesia clerk back to lock in the agreed date.
  4. Only after the date is locked in, fill up the “Out of OT Work Request Form” via FormSG:
    Open Out of OT Request Form (FormSG) ↗
The form is also on the intranet: Departments → Clinical Departments → Department of Anaesthesia → eForms → “Out of OT Request Form”.
Arranging MDPU Admissions
  • Check MDPU availability: open the Calendar tab (top left) → type “NUH Medical Day Procedural Unit” under the Dept tab → select the date. Usually max 6 patients per day.
  • Order MDPU + procedure under discharge orders; call AMU2 PSA @ 67722282.
MDPU — Calendar tab, select date to view the day’s list
MDPU — daily list (max ~6 patients)
Arranging Elective Admissions

Acute Lower GI Bleeding (LGIB)

ACG Clinical Guideline — Sengupta et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2023;118:208–231

Management Algorithm
Acute haematochezia
Resuscitate & risk-assess
2 large-bore IV · FBC, coagulation, UEC, LFT, G&S · transfuse to Hb ≥7 g/dL (≥8 g/dL if cardiac disease)
Hold anticoagulants · stop NSAIDs · continue aspirin if secondary prevention
Haemodynamically unstable or ongoing brisk bleeding?
HR >100 · SBP <100 · continuing haematochezia
Yes — unstable
CT mesenteric angiography first
Detects bleeding ≥0.3 mL/min. Fast and widely available — do not delay for bowel prep.
Consider an upper GI source (~15% of apparent LGIB) — OGD if suspected
Active blush
Angiography
+ IR embolisation
No blush
Aim for preparation and colonoscopy
Consider surgical consultation
No — stable
Non-urgent inpatient colonoscopy
After bowel prep.
Urgent (<24H) colonoscopy is not superior.
Treat the source
Diverticular → clips, band ligation, APC or adrenaline injection · Angioectasia → APC · Colitis → treat the underlying cause
Rebleeding → repeat colonoscopy → angiography ± embolisation → surgery
Common Causes
CauseFeaturesFrequency
Diverticular bleedingPainless, large-volume, bright red; right-sided more common; self-limited in 80%30–40%
Colitis (ischaemic, IBD, infective)Abdominal pain ± diarrhoea; ischaemic = watershed areas~20%
Angioectasia / AVMPainless; older patients; CKD, cardiac disease, Heyde's syndrome~8%
Post-polypectomy bleedAcute (procedural) or delayed up to 14 days~8%
Colorectal neoplasiaIntermittent, mixed with stool~5%
Haemorrhoids / anorectalBright red coating stool, post-defaecation — diagnosis of exclusionVariable
⚠ Massive UGIBHaematochezia + haemodynamic instability = UGIB until proven otherwise. HR >100 or SBP <100 → OGD first, not colonoscopy.~15% of apparent LGIB
Initial Assessment & Resuscitation
  • IV access × 2 large-bore; FBC, coagulation, UEC, LFT, G&S; crossmatch if ongoing bleed
  • Haemodynamic instability: resuscitate first — transfuse to Hb ≥7 g/dL (≥8 g/dL if cardiac disease)
  • Hold anticoagulants; discontinue NSAIDs; continue aspirin if secondary CV prevention
ScenarioApproachRationale / Evidence
Haemodynamically UNSTABLE or ongoing massive bleedCT mesenteric angiography (CTMA) first. Active blush on CTMA → conventional angiography ± IR embolisation. No blush → proceed to colonoscopy; consider surgical consultation. Consider an upper GI source (~15% of apparent LGIB) — OGD if suspected.CTMA fast, widely available, detects bleeding ≥0.3 mL/min. Do not delay for colonoscopy prep.
Haemodynamically STABLENon-urgent inpatient colonoscopy. Urgent colonoscopy (<24H) is NOT superior to 2–3 days. Bowel prep required.ACG 2023: urgent colonoscopy has NOT shown reduced rebleeding, surgery, or mortality vs non-urgent. Reserve for high-risk (ongoing CT blush, anticoagulated).
Post-polypectomy bleedAcute: reverse anticoagulation; colonoscopy for clip/APC. Delayed (1–14 days): usually self-limiting; colonoscopy if haemodynamically significant.Endoscopic therapy feasible and preferred over IR if accessible.
Endoscopic Therapy
  • Diverticular: APC, clips, band ligation, or epinephrine injection at bleeding vessel
  • Angioectasia: APC preferred; rebleeding rate high (34–46% at 3 years)
  • Colitis: Treat underlying cause; endoscopic therapy generally not indicated
Post-Discharge Management
  • Continue aspirin if taken for established cardiovascular disease (secondary prevention)
  • Resume anticoagulation once bleeding has definitively stopped

Gastroenterology

Obscure GI Bleeding

ACG Clinical Guideline — Gerson et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2015;110:1265–1287

Algorithm — Suspected Small Bowel Bleeding
Management approach to suspected small bowel bleeding

Source: A Practical Guide to the Evaluation of Small Bowel Bleeding. Mayo Clinic Proceedings. Reproduced for educational purposes.

Terminology
  • Small bowel bleeding: Bleeding distal to ampulla of Vater, proximal to ileocaecal valve. ~5–10% of all GI bleeding.
  • Obscure GI haemorrhage (OGIB): Bleeding with no source identified after complete evaluation of upper GI, small bowel, and colon. Diagnosis of exclusion.
  • Potential small bowel bleeding: After normal OGD and colonoscopy, before small bowel evaluation is complete.
Aetiology by Age
Age <40Age >40Rare (any age)
IBD (Crohn's disease)Angioectasia / angiodysplasia (most common)Portal hypertensive enteropathy
Meckel's diverticulumNSAID-induced ulcersHaemangioma / blue rubber bleb
Dieulafoy's lesionDieulafoy's lesionHereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia
Small bowel neoplasia (GIST, lymphoma, carcinoid)Small bowel neoplasiaAorto-enteric fistula
Polyposis syndromes (Peutz-Jeghers, FAP)Polyposis syndromesHeyde's syndrome (aortic stenosis + angioectasia)
First Step: Bidirectional Endoscopy

Before labelling as "small bowel", perform OGD and colonoscopy. Up to 25% of suspected small bowel bleeds have upper or lower sources on repeat endoscopy.

Imaging Modalities
ModalityWhen to UseKey Points
Video Capsule Endoscopy (VCE)Stable patient; first-line small bowel evaluation after bidirectional endoscopyDiagnostic yield 38–83%. Highest yield: overt bleeding, Hb <10, within 48–72H of episode. Main limitation: no therapeutic capability; capsule retention ~1.5% (higher in Crohn's).
CT Mesenteric Angiography (CTMA)Unstable patient with active overt bleeding; if VCE not available urgentlyDetects bleeding ≥0.3 mL/min. Guides conventional angiography ± embolisation. Sensitivity ~89%, specificity ~85%. If CTMA negative, conventional angiography unlikely to be positive.
CT Enterography (CTE)After negative VCE; suspected small bowel mass/tumourBetter than VCE for mural-based masses (detects 9/9 vs 3/9 tumours in one study). Complementary to VCE — may miss mucosal erosions, ulcers, and vascular lesions. Yield ~40% overall.
Balloon Enteroscopy (Double-balloon / Single-balloon)After positive VCE — for therapy; if VCE contraindicated; high suspicion despite negative VCEDiagnostic yield 60–80%; therapeutic 40–73%. Antegrade (oral) or retrograde (rectal) approach. Time-consuming; antegrade may require GA support.
Conventional AngiographyAfter positive CTMA; haemodynamically unstableRequires active bleeding ≥0.5–1.0 mL/min for detection. Allows embolisation. Do NOT use as a diagnostic test without active bleeding. Yield ~50%; complication rate up to 10%.
Surgical managementLast resortReserve for patients with recurrent bleeding requiring multiple transfusions after a comprehensive negative evaluation. Mark the lesion (tattoo / angiographic dye) to guide resection.
Management Algorithm
Clinical ScenarioRecommended Approach
Haemodynamically unstable + active overt bleedResuscitate. CTMA first. CTMA positive → conventional angiography ± embolisation. CTMA negative + still bleeding → urgent enteroscopy or surgery.
Stable + active overt bleedVCE within 48–72H of episode after negative bidirectional endoscopy (highest yield during active/recent bleed). VCE positive → balloon enteroscopy for therapy. VCE negative → CTE if mass suspected.
Occult bleeding (IDA ± FOB+, no active bleed)VCE after negative bidirectional endoscopy. VCE positive → enteroscopy. VCE negative → CTE if mass suspected. Conservative iron supplementation if no source found.
Risk for capsule retention (e.g. Crohn's, previous small bowel obstruction, previous abdominal surgery with concern for adhesions, radiation enteritis)CTE/CTAP first to exclude obstruction. If clear → patency capsule → then VCE.
Negative comprehensive evaluationOvert: repeat VCE; provocative angiography; Meckel's scan if <40. Occult: conservative iron supplementation; re-investigate if escalates.
Treatment
  • Angioectasia: APC (argon plasma coagulation) is primary modality. Rebleeding rates 34–46% at 36 months despite treatment.
  • Refractory angioectasia: Somatostatin analogues (octreotide LAR / lanreotide) reduce transfusion requirements. Thalidomide (antiangiogenic) has evidence in refractory cases.
  • Heyde's syndrome (aortic stenosis + angioectasia): AVR may resolve angioectasia-related bleeding.
  • Surgery: Last resort. Tattoo/angiographic dye injection to localise lesion for resection.

Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs)

Kirchheiner et al., Eur J Clin Pharmacol 2009 · Graham & Tansel, Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol 2018 · NUH Formulary

Omeprazole 20 mg is the reference standard. Potency and the “equivalent dose” column below are both expressed relative to omeprazole (i.e. the dose giving the same acid-suppressing effect as omeprazole) — useful when switching agents. Take 30–60 min before meals.

DrugPotency vs omeprazoleEquivalent dose (vs omeprazole)Key notes
Omeprazole1× (reference)20 mg = referenceFirst-generation reference PPI. Wide inter-individual variability from CYP2C19 metabolism.
Esomeprazole~1.6×20 mg ≈ omeprazole 32 mgS-isomer of omeprazole; more consistent suppression. Preferred IV agent for UGIB.
Rabeprazole~1.8×20 mg ≈ omeprazole 36 mgFastest onset; least CYP2C19-dependent of the classic PPIs. Useful in H. pylori regimens.
Dexlansoprazole~1.6×30 mg ≈ esomeprazole 20 mgDual delayed-release — meal-timing independent; useful for nocturnal breakthrough.
Lansoprazole~0.9×30 mg ≈ omeprazole 27 mgSimilar potency to omeprazole. ODT (dispersible) — useful for NGT / dysphagia.
Pantoprazole~0.23× (weakest)40 mg ≈ omeprazole 9 mgLeast potent per mg, but fewest CYP interactions — preferred with clopidogrel / polypharmacy.
Vonoprazan (P-CAB)≫ any PPI (not a PPI)20 mg ≫ any standard PPI dosePotassium-competitive acid blocker. Faster, stronger, longer-lasting and more CYP-independent than any PPI. Superior H. pylori eradication in Asian populations.

Potency ranking: Vonoprazan ≫ Esomeprazole ≈ Rabeprazole ≈ Dexlansoprazole > Omeprazole ≈ Lansoprazole > Pantoprazole. CYP2C19 poor metabolisers achieve higher levels of omeprazole/esomeprazole/lansoprazole; rabeprazole and vonoprazan are least affected.

Why BD dosing helps: PPIs only inhibit actively-secreting pumps and have a short half-life (~1–2H) while pumps regenerate continuously — a single morning dose leaves some pumps uninhibited (nocturnal acid breakthrough). Splitting the same daily dose into pre-breakfast + pre-dinner gives more sustained 24-h suppression. Consider BD for refractory GERD, erosive oesophagitis, nocturnal breakthrough, peptic ulcer healing and H. pylori eradication. If still failing → switch to esomeprazole/rabeprazole, dexlansoprazole, or vonoprazan.
PPI by Indication
IndicationDose & DurationNotes
Acute UGIB — post-haemostasisIV esomeprazole 80 mg bolus + 8 mg/hr × 72H (Forrest Ia–IIb) → PO 20 mg BD × 4–8 wkLow-risk lesions (Forrest IIc/III): oral standard dose adequate.
Gastric ulcerPPI 20 mg BD × 8 wk (e.g. omeprazole 20 mg BD)Mandatory OGD at 8 wk to confirm healing / exclude malignancy. Biopsy all GU. Eradicate H. pylori if positive.
Duodenal ulcerPPI 20 mg BD × 4 wkH. pylori eradication is curative. No routine follow-up OGD for uncomplicated DU.
Erosive GERDPPI 20 mg BD × 8 wk; maintenance if grade C/DStep down to lowest effective dose. Screen for Barrett’s; OGD to confirm grade.
Non-erosive GERD (NERD)PPI 20 mg OD or on-demand; 4–8 wk trial~50–60% response. If inadequate: optimise timing + lifestyle → pH-impedance study.
Stress ulcer prophylaxisPPI 20 mg BD IV/PO; ICU / high-risk period onlyIndications: MV >48H, coagulopathy, severe burns, TBI, spinal injury, hepatic/renal failure. Stop at step-down.
NUH: IV PPI for UGIB = esomeprazole 80 mg bolus + 8 mg/hr. Review and stop PPIs at ward transfer if no ongoing indication (excess C. difficile risk).
Laxatives

ACG 2021 · AGA 2023 · BSG/ACPGBI 2024

ClassAgent · DoseIndications & Cautions
Bulk-formingPsyllium (ispaghula husk) 5–10 g OD/BD with water. Onset 12–72H.First-line for mild–moderate constipation; also helps IBS-C bloating. Needs adequate hydration. Avoid in opioid-induced constipation or suspected obstruction.
Osmotic (maintenance)Forlax (macrogol / PEG 3350) 1–3 sachets OD (each in ~125 mL water). Onset 24–48H.Preferred maintenance osmotic (AGA 2023) — better tolerated than lactulose, less bloating.
Osmotic (lavage)PEG (large-volume) per bowel-prep regimenMainly for colonoscopy bowel preparation.
OsmoticLactulose 15–30 mL BD. Onset 24–48H.Constipation; also hepatic encephalopathy (titrate to 2–3 soft stools/day). More bloating/flatulence than macrogol.
StimulantBisacodyl 5–10 mg ON PO or 10 mg PR (PR onset 15–60 min); Senna 7.5–15 mg ON; Sodium picosulphateShort-term / rescue use when osmotics insufficient. Avoid prolonged continuous use. Senna often combined with an osmotic in opioid-induced constipation. Sodium picosulphate is a bowel-prep component (Picolax/Picoprep).
Prokinetic (5-HT₄)Prucalopride (Resolor) 2 mg OD (1 mg if elderly / renal impairment)Selective 5-HT₄ agonist → pan-enteric prokinesis. Strong recommendation (ACG/AGA) for chronic constipation after first-line laxatives fail. Generally well tolerated; good cardiac safety.
IBAT inhibitorElobixibat (Goofice) 10 mg OD before breakfast (range 5–15 mg)Inhibits the ileal bile acid transporter (IBAT / ASBT) in the terminal ileum → less bile acid reabsorption → more bile acids reach the colon, stimulating colonic secretion and motility; minimally absorbed (acts locally). Onset within hours. For chronic constipation, including slow-transit / refractory cases when osmotic ± stimulant laxatives are inadequate. Take before a meal (bile-acid flow is meal-stimulated). SE: abdominal pain, diarrhoea. May modestly lower LDL cholesterol.
Functional GI — Antispasmodics, Antiflatulents & Prokinetics
DrugClass · DoseIndication & Cautions
Hyoscine butylbromide (Buscopan)Anticholinergic antispasmodic · 10–20 mg TDS–QDS POIBS-D cramps, post-prandial pain. Does not cross BBB (fewer CNS effects). Avoid in glaucoma, urinary retention, myasthenia gravis.
Mebeverine (Duspatalin)Direct smooth-muscle relaxant · 135 mg TDS (20 min before meals)IBS with pain/spasm. BSG first-line antispasmodic. No anticholinergic side effects — better tolerated.
Meteospasmyl (alverine + simethicone)Antispasmodic + antiflatulent · 1 cap TDS (alverine 60 mg + simethicone 300 mg)IBS with bloating + pain — useful when bloating is prominent alongside spasm.
Librax (chlordiazepoxide + clidinium)Benzodiazepine + anticholinergic · 1–2 tab TDS–QDSIBS with prominent anxiety + IBS-D. Short-term only (benzodiazepine dependence risk). Avoid in the elderly.
DomperidoneD2 antagonist; peripheral prokinetic (no EPS) · 10 mg TDS (30 min AC), max 30 mg/day, ≤4 wkNausea, bloating, post-prandial fullness, gastroparesis. QTc prolongation — contraindicated with prolonged QTc, cardiac disease, or CYP3A4 inhibitors (azoles, macrolides, diltiazem). ECG if cardiac risk factors.
Simethicone / dimethiconeAnti-foaming agent · 40–125 mg TDS–QDS after mealsBloating, flatulence, post-op gas pain. Added to PEG bowel prep; pre-endoscopy defoaming agent. Safe in pregnancy and children.
Peppermint oil (Colpermin)L-menthol Ca-channel antagonist · 1–2 enteric-coated caps TDS before mealsIBS with pain + bloating. ACG strong recommendation. Do not crush/chew (→ GORD). Avoid in hiatal hernia / GORD-dominant symptoms.
Antiemetics — When to Choose What

MASCC Antiemetic Guidelines 2023 · NUH Formulary

Dopamine antagonists (metoclopramide, domperidone) for functional / gastroparetic nausea; 5-HT3 antagonists (ondansetron) for post-op, chemotherapy-induced or refractory nausea; antihistamines for vestibular / motion-related nausea and pregnancy.

DrugClass · DoseIndication & Cautions
Metoclopramide (Maxalon)D2 antagonist + 5-HT4 agonist · 10 mg TDS PO/IV/IM, max 30 mg/day (≤5 d IV, ≤12 wk PO)First-line for gastroparesis, post-op nausea, functional dyspepsia. Extrapyramidal effects (akathisia, dystonia, tardive dyskinesia) — higher risk in young women and elderly. Avoid in Parkinson’s. Crosses BBB.
DomperidoneD2 antagonist, peripheral only (no EPS) · 10 mg TDS (30 min AC), max 30 mg/day, ≤4 wkFunctional nausea, gastroparesis, post-prandial fullness. Preferred over metoclopramide when CNS effects are a concern. QTc prolongation — contraindicated with CYP3A4 inhibitors, cardiac disease, hepatic impairment.
Ondansetron5-HT3 antagonist · 4–8 mg BD–TDS PO/IV (slow over 15 min); max 32 mg/day IV; reduce in hepatic impairmentPreferred for PONV, CINV, refractory nausea, Parkinson’s (no D2 block), high EPS risk. Not a prokinetic. QTc prolongation (esp. IV/high-dose); constipation; serotonin syndrome risk with serotonergic drugs.
PromethazineH1 antihistamine + anticholinergic · 12.5–25 mg TDS–QDS PO/IM/IV (slow, diluted)Vestibular / motion-sickness nausea; PONV (2nd-line); hyperemesis gravidarum (1st-line). Significant sedation; anticholinergic effects. Contraindicated in Parkinson’s.
DexamethasoneGlucocorticoid · 4–8 mg IV/PO OD–BD; CINV 8–20 mg pre-chemoCINV (moderately/highly emetogenic — with ondansetron); PONV prophylaxis; delayed CINV (days 2–5). Monitor glucose; short courses only.

CLIF-C ACLF Score

Jalan et al., J Hepatol 2014;61:1038–1047 · CANONIC cohort (n=1,343)

Predicts 28-day and 90-day mortality in ACLF. Enter values from the patient's current assessment. Organ failure thresholds per EASL-CLIF criteria.

Organ Failure Thresholds (EASL-CLIF)
OrganDysfunction (score 1)Score 2Failure (score 3; kidney = ≥2)
Liver (bilirubin μmol/L)<103104–206>206
Kidney (creatinine μmol/L)<175176–310 = FAILURE>310 or RRT = FAILURE
Brain (West Haven grade)01–23–4 = FAILURE
Coagulation (INR)<2.02.0–2.4≥2.5 = FAILURE
Circulation (MAP mmHg)≥70<70Vasopressors = FAILURE
Respiratory (PaO₂/FiO₂)>300201–300≤200 = FAILURE
ACLF GradeOrgan Failures28-day Mortality90-day Mortality
No ACLFNone<5%~10%
Grade 11~20%~40%
Grade 22~40%~60%
Grade 3≥3>70%~90%

Formula: Score = 10 × [0.33 × OF_score + 0.04 × age + 0.63 × ln(WBC) − 2 × ln(creatinine g/dL) + 0.03 × bilirubin mg/dL]. For clinical guidance only.

Creatinine Clearance (Cockcroft-Gault)

CrCl (mL/min) = [(140 − age) × weight (kg) × (0.85 if female)] ÷ (0.814 × creatinine µmol/L). Estimates renal function for drug dosing (e.g. DOAC hold durations). Use actual body weight (consider ideal/adjusted weight in obesity).
